It also makes new skills ( skills new ), installs them from git, validates them, and can pin one as a slash command. skills skill prints a guide built into the binary, so an agent can learn the whole tool with one command. My laptop is also a security camera I can watch my laptop's camera and listen to its microphone from my phone, from anywhere, and nothing is exposed to the internet. It works over Tailscale only. There's nothing to forward on the router, and the server listens only on the machine's Tailscale addresses and refuses anything outside the tailnet. You turn it on in Settings › Security Camera, open the address on your phone, and add it to the home screen for a full screen app. The camera only opens when the first viewer arrives and closes about ten seconds after the last one leaves, so it's off while nobody's watching. Up to eight phones at once. By default only devices signed in to my own Tailscale account are allowed, checked with tailscale whois , so someone else on a shared tailnet gets refused and logged. And the camera's activity light is always on while it streams. It's never hidden or faked, which I think is the right call. Tailscale shows up everywhere else too. Settings › Tailscale handles devices, exit nodes, SSH and file sharing, and in Files you can right click a file and choose Send over Tailscale to Taildrop it to any of my devices. Keeping it all alive You should see the size of the CHANGELOG for cloudwerx-os. It's pushing 3,000 lines, and it's come a REAL long way. I work on it every day. From any of my many connected devices I can push a new PR and sync it onto any of my hardware with a single click. I wrote an updater for the whole OS that handles the AUR packages, the kernel and everything else, and it takes a snapshot before it touches anything, so I can roll back when (not if) I mess something up. I also have a Telegram bot, and a Tasks page that's basically cron with a user interface. I can set up a job that makes Claude Code go hunt for the coolest open source GitHub projects from the last week, formats a nice rich message and sends it to me on Telegram. Every week, completely automated. I wake up on Monday to a newsletter that my computer wrote for me. I have a similar system on my NAS called JONAS (Joint Operations NAS Admin System). That's a story for another day. Let's just say Synology wishes it had this many features. Things I've built in the last three years CLOUDWERX OS isn't the only thing that came out of the last 3 years. My portfolio at cloudwerxlab.com is a descent through a mycelium network with 15 projects in it, and a lot of them run on my NAS behind Cloudflare tunnels. A few I'm especially fond of: X-Tracks ( x-tracks.app ) is a self-hosted music archive. Paste a Spotify or YouTube Music link and it archives the tracks as MP3, FLAC, Opus or M4A with real metadata and artwork. No Spotify login or developer key. It has 29 visualizers, 20 of them audio reactive (way nicer than Winamp ever was), and you can write your own GLSL shaders in a Visualization Studio. It also has DJ X, an AI agent. Give it one prompt and it researches the web, searches YouTube Music and Spotify, downloads the music, builds you a playlist with generated artwork and starts playing it. It can even write new visualizers. It's still in development. Terminaut ( terminaut.app ) is mission control for every server you run. Start and stop them in batches, watch their output stream live, and drop into a real interactive shell. Pretty Hooker ( Docker Hub ) turns webhooks into desktop notifications for your homelab. Point Uptime Kuma, Grafana, GitHub, Sonarr, Home Assistant or a plain curl at it. R2Up ( r2up.cloudwerxlab.com ) uploads past Cloudflare's 300 MB dashboard limit by chunking files into S3 multipart uploads, all in your browser. CapGen ( capgen.cloudwerxlab.com ) builds, cleans and captions image datasets for LoRA training. SugarStem separates stems locally, so your audio never leaves your computer. Cinnaroll is a theme browser for Linux Mint. TaskPunk is a markdown first task manager. And there's a whole desktop that runs in a browser tab , with a tiny AI unicorn who can redecorate it. I run a pile of self hosted goodies on the homelab too, Immich among them, plus the NAS agent I keep teasing. So, why do this? Because I could. That's the real answer, and it's the answer that would've made 12-year old me, running a BBS on a phone line, lose his mind. I spent decades inside systems somebody else decided were good enough. Then it turned out I could just... build the thing. The tools got good enough, and so did I. My OS is everything I've ever wanted from a computer. It does what I say, it looks how I want, it tells me when it's broken, and it never once asked me to sign into a Microsoft account to look at a calculator. Stories for another day I've got a lot more where this came from, and I plan to write them all up here. A few teasers, in no particular order: How I run ablated open weights models on a custom VPS for the times I want to do things the frontier labs won't let me. (Shh.) How I got a root shell on my DJI drone, which let me fly it literally inside the clouds, and very nearly visit outer space. My custom astrophotography rig, built around a hacked DSLR. The MAME cabinet I built from a classic Mortal Kombat II arcade machine, with custom vinyl side art, a custom desktop living inside it running a custom frontend, and a totally customized control panel. JONAS, the admin agent that runs my NAS. Synology wishes. What I got up to in AOL chatrooms in the early 2000s, with classic remote access tools disguised as images, and the very bad people it was aimed at. Maybe I'll tell that one with a drink in my hand. My wife, Sizzlebop , builds a ton of her own projects too, and I get to live next to all of it. Go follow her on GitHub and on dev.to . You won't regret it. I'll write more of these. There's plenty left to tell, like how the theme engine works, how the plugin system works and how I run a small army of agents without losing my mind. If any of this sounds like your kind of fun, say hi. I'm genuinely curious what you'd build. Ty CLOUDWERX LAB, Digital Food for the Analog Soul cloudwerxlab.com · github.com/CLOUDWERX-DEV

title: The Three Clocks of a Crypto Swap: Why Timing Matters More Than Most Users Realize
summary: TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN. tronseven.com A crypto swap looks like a single action. You select a token, enter an amount, review the exchange rate, approve the transaction, and wait for the result. But from a technical perspective, a swap is not one event. It is a sequence of events operating on three different timelines. And understanding those timelines explains several problems that crypto users encounter: outdated quotes, unexpected execution results, confusing wallet prompts, and transactions that appear to be stuck. Let's explore this from a developer's perspective, using the TRON ecosystem as a practical example. The first clock: The quote has a lifetime Imagine a user wants to exchange USDT for TRX. The application displays an estimated output amount. The user reviews it, switches to another browser tab, checks a message, and returns thirty seconds later. Should the application still treat the original quote as valid? Not necessarily. A displayed exchange rate represents a snapshot of market conditions at a particular moment. Depending on the liquidity mechanism and execution path, the underlying conditions can change. Several factors matter: Available liquidity. Token price movements. Trading activity. Price impact. Slippage tolerance. Changes in the execution route. This creates an important distinction between a quoted result and an executed result. A well-designed swap interface should make that distinction understandable. For developers, this means thinking about quote expiration, recalculation, minimum acceptable output, and the information displayed immediately before transaction approval. The objective isn't to promise that every quote will remain unchanged. It's to prevent users from confusing an estimate with a guaranteed settlement amount. The second clock: Wallet approval is a separate event The next timeline begins when the user interacts with their wallet. This is where application design becomes particularly interesting. A swap interface and a wallet are separate components. The application can request an action, but the wallet controls the user's authorization. That creates several possible situations: The user approves the transaction immediately. The user rejects the request. The wallet takes time to respond. The user switches accounts. The connection is interrupted. The application receives an unexpected response. A common UX mistake is treating the appearance of a wallet confirmation window as evidence that the transaction has been completed. It isn't. A wallet approval is not the same thing as blockchain execution. Developers should represent these states separately and communicate them clearly. For example, an application might distinguish between: Preparing the transaction. Waiting for wallet authorization. Transaction submitted. Transaction confirmed. Transaction failed. These distinctions might seem small, but they significantly improve the user's understanding of what is happening. They also make debugging easier because developers can identify which stage actually failed. The third clock: Blockchain settlement The third timeline belongs to the network itself. Once a transaction is broadcast, the application must wait for blockchain-level confirmation rather than simply assuming that submission means success. This distinction is especially important in wallet-connected applications. A transaction can be submitted successfully but still encounter execution problems. A user might also close the interface before the application has updated its status. That is why transaction tracking should not depend entirely on the browser session remaining active. A more resilient design uses the transaction identifier to retrieve the actual result from the blockchain. On TRON, TRONSCAN provides a convenient way to inspect publicly available transaction information. This creates a useful separation of responsibilities: The interface communicates the current status. The wallet handles authorization. The blockchain records execution. The explorer provides an independent way to inspect the transaction. For developers, this is a reminder that the frontend should never become the ultimate source of truth for blockchain execution. What happens when the three clocks disagree? Here is a practical scenario. A user opens a swap interface and receives a quote. They take some time to review it. Meanwhile, market conditions change. They return and approve the transaction. The wallet submits the request, but the network takes additional time to process it. From the user's perspective, this might look like one slow operation. From the application's perspective, however, three separate processes have occurred: Quote lifecycle: The original estimate may no longer reflect current conditions. Authorization lifecycle: The wallet has handled the user's approval. Settlement lifecycle: The network still needs to process and confirm execution. If the application communicates these processes poorly, users may repeatedly click buttons, submit duplicate requests, or assume that funds have disappeared. Good interface architecture should prevent this confusion. Some practical design principles include: Refresh quotes when appropriate. Clearly display the estimated output. Explain wallet authorization requests. Disable duplicate submissions while a transaction is pending. Preserve transaction identifiers. Provide a way to inspect transaction status. Distinguish failed transactions from transactions that are still pending. These aren't cosmetic improvements. They are part of making blockchain applications more predictable. Why TRON makes this discussion particularly relevant The TRON ecosystem has its own infrastructure considerations. TRC-20 tokens, wallet integrations, smart contracts, Energy, and Bandwidth all influence how applications interact with the network. Developers building around TRON need to understand that transaction costs and execution behavior are connected to network resources. Energy is particularly important when interacting with smart contracts. A user who understands token balances but has no idea how network resources work may find the transaction experience confusing. This is why a good swap interface should make network-related information understandable without forcing every user to become a blockchain engineer. The challenge is to keep the experience simple while preserving the technical details that matter. Applying these principles to TronSeven One project worth exploring in the TRON swap ecosystem is TronSeven. TronSeven is a non-custodial token exchange focused on TRON assets and TRC-20 tokens, including USDT and USDC. The platform lists integrations with TronLink, Trust Wallet, and WalletConnect. It also provides public smart contract information and a TRONSCAN link, allowing interested users to investigate its on-chain activity independently. Another interesting aspect is its use of TRON Energy to address swap-related network costs. For anyone evaluating a swap application, these are useful starting points for examining how wallet connectivity, contract execution, and network resources come together. You can explore the platform here: https://tronseven.com As with any blockchain application, users should independently examine contract information, understand wallet authorization requests, and verify transactions rather than relying exclusively on interface descriptions. A developer's checklist for better swap interfaces Before considering a swap interface production-ready, I would ask the following questions: Quote management Can users distinguish estimates from executed results? Are outdated quotes handled appropriately? Is slippage explained? Wallet interaction Are authorization and execution separate states? Are rejected requests handled properly? Can the interface recover from a disconnected wallet? Blockchain interaction Is transaction status retrieved from reliable network data? Can users independently inspect transaction identifiers? Are pending and failed transactions clearly distinguished? Network resources Are Energy and Bandwidth considerations communicated? Does the interface explain unexpected network-related errors? User experience Can duplicate submissions be prevented? Are errors understandable? Does the interface remain useful when the browser session is interrupted? These questions apply far beyond TRON. They are relevant to almost every wallet-connected application that interacts with blockchain networks. Final thoughts A crypto swap may look like a simple button, but the engineering behind it involves multiple independent systems operating on different timelines. The quote represents market conditions. The wallet represents user authorization. The blockchain represents actual execution. When these three timelines are handled correctly, the result is a more understandable, predictable, and trustworthy user experience. I think this is one of the most important directions for the next generation of crypto applications: making complex blockchain operations feel simple without hiding the technical realities behind them. Because in Web3, simplicity should never come at the expense of transparency.

title: How do I automate functional software testing?
summary: Short answer: decide which behaviors matter most, check each one at the lowest layer where it actually lives, give your tests predictable data and fake versions of outside services, then make your CI pipeline run them on every change. That's the whole loop of automated functional testing . The rest of this post walks through it with a small, concrete example, because "automate your tests" is easy advice to give and surprisingly hard to act on when you're staring at an empty test folder. The example is a basic online store with a cart and discount coupons. Swap in your own product as you read. The steps don't change much. Start with a list, not a tool Most people open a browser tab and start comparing frameworks. That's backwards. The tool matters a lot less than knowing what you're going to test. Grab a doc and write down three things: The flows that make or lose money, like signup, login, adding to cart, checkout and refunds The last ten or so bugs that reached production Anything you or your QA folks re-check by hand before every release For our store, the list might start like this: a customer can log in, add items, apply a valid coupon, get a clear error for an expired coupon, and pay with a saved card. Five items. That's plenty for a first pass. Write the expected behavior in plain words Before any code, write each item as a short scenario. A simple format works well: Given a cart with two mugs at 50.00 each When the customer applies coupon SAVE10 Then the total is 90.00 Given a coupon that expired yesterday When the customer applies it Then they get an "expired coupon" error and the total doesn't change This feels like busywork. It isn't. Half the arguments about whether a test is "right" turn out to be arguments about what the feature should do, and it's much cheaper to settle those in a sentence than in a pull request. Decide where each check belongs Now ask where each behavior actually lives in your system. The discount math happens on the server. So test it by calling the API directly. You don't need a browser to confirm that 100 minus 10% is 90, and a browser test for it will break whenever someone renames a button. The fact that a customer can get from the product page to a paid order is a journey that crosses the UI, the API and the payment step. That one deserves a browser test. For our store, the split ends up like this: Scenario Layer Why Valid coupon applies the right discount API Pure business logic, fast to check Expired coupon is rejected API Error handling lives in the backend Login with wrong password fails API Same reason Customer checks out with a saved card UI The full journey is what matters Three API tests and one UI test. That ratio holds up well as suites grow. A worked example at the API layer Here's what the coupon tests might look like in Python with pytest and requests. Any language and HTTP client will do the same job. import uuid import requests BASE = "http://localhost:8000" def new_customer ( ) : email = f "qa-{uuid.uuid4().hex[:8]}@example.test" r = requests . post ( f "{BASE}/users" , json = { "email" : email , "password" : "Passw0rd!" } ) assert r . status_code == 201 return { "Authorization" : f "Bearer {r.json()['token']}" } def test_save10_takes_ten_percent_off ( ) : headers = new_customer ( ) requests . post ( f "{BASE}/cart/items" , json = { "sku" : "MUG-01" , "qty" : 2 } , headers = headers ) r = requests . post ( f "{BASE}/cart/coupon" , json = { "code" : "SAVE10" } , headers = headers ) assert r . status_code == 200 assert r . json ( ) [ "total" ] == "90.00" def test_expired_coupon_is_rejected ( ) : headers = new_customer ( ) requests . post ( f "{BASE}/cart/items" , json = { "sku" : "MUG-01" , "qty" : 2 } , headers = headers ) r = requests . post ( f "{BASE}/cart/coupon" , json = { "code" : "OLD5" } , headers = headers ) assert r . status_code == 422 assert r . json ( ) [ "error" ] == "coupon_expired" assert r . json ( ) [ "total" ] == "100.00" A few things worth pointing out, because they're where beginners usually slip: Every test creates its own customer with a random email. No test depends on another one having run first. Each test checks one behavior and says exactly what "correct" means. "Status is 200" alone would pass even if the discount were wrong. The expired coupon test also checks that the total didn't change. Bugs love to hide in the "nothing should happen" cases. Handling the database and outside services Those tests assume two things exist: a product called MUG-01 priced at 50.00, and a coupon called OLD5 that has already expired. Don't create those by hand in a shared staging database and hope nobody touches them. Someone will. Put them in a seed script that runs before the suite, against a database that exists only for testing. A throwaway container started in CI is the usual approach. Fresh data every run means a failure points at your code, not at whatever a colleague did on staging last Thursday. Outside services need the same treatment. If checkout calls a payment provider, your test suite shouldn't depend on that provider's sandbox being up. Replace it with a mock that returns realistic responses, including the unpleasant ones like a declined card or a timeout. Then keep a handful of separate checks that hit the real sandbox on a schedule, so you still find out if their API changes. If writing mocks by hand sounds tedious, it is. Some teams record real traffic between their service and its dependencies and replay it as mocks, which saves a lot of typing and keeps the mocks closer to reality. Adding a few UI tests Once the API layer is covered, add browser tests for the journeys a customer can't live without. Here's the checkout one in Playwright: import { test , expect } from '@playwright/test' ; test ( 'customer can check out with a saved card' , async ( { page } ) => { await page . goto ( '/login' ) ; await page . getByLabel ( 'Email' ) . fill ( 'saved-card@example.test' ) ; await page . getByLabel ( 'Password' ) . fill ( 'Passw0rd!' ) ; await page . getByRole ( 'button' , { name : 'Log in' } ) . click ( ) ; await page . goto ( '/products/mug-01' ) ; await page . getByRole ( 'button' , { name : 'Add to cart' } ) . click ( ) ; await page . getByRole ( 'link' , { name : 'Checkout' } ) . click ( ) ; await page . getByRole ( 'button' , { name : 'Pay now' } ) . click ( ) ; await expect ( page . getByText ( 'Order confirmed' ) ) . toBeVisible ( ) ; } ) ; Notice it finds elements by their label and role, not by CSS classes. Designers change class names all the time. They rarely change a button that says "Pay now" without also changing what it does. Keep this layer small. Ten to twenty UI tests covering real journeys will tell you more than a hundred that click every button on every page. Getting it into CI Tests that only run on someone's laptop stop running. Put them in your pipeline so they run without anyone having to remember. A minimal GitHub Actions setup looks like this: name : functional-tests on : [ pull_request ] jobs : api-tests : runs-on : ubuntu-latest steps : - uses : actions/checkout@v4 - run : docker compose up -d db app - run : python scripts/seed_test_data.py - run : pip install -r requirements-test.txt - run : pytest tests/api -q Start there. Once that's stable, add the UI tests on merge to your main branch, the full regression set before releases, and a nightly run against staging. Keep the pull request stage under about ten minutes, or people will merge before it finishes and the whole thing loses its point. Keeping the suite alive Writing the first tests is the fun part. Keeping them useful is the actual job. When a test turns flaky, fix it or delete it that week. A retry button teaches the team that red builds don't mean anything, and that lesson is very hard to unlearn. When a production bug slips through, write the test that would have caught it before you write the fix. Your suite slowly becomes a record of everything that has ever gone wrong, which is exactly what you want it to be. And review test code in pull requests the same way you review everything else. A test nobody understands is a test nobody will fix when it breaks. FAQs What's the first functional test I should automate? Pick the flow that would hurt most if it broke tomorrow. For most products that's login or checkout. Automate the happy path and one or two common failures, get it running in CI, then move on to the next one. Do I need to know how to code to automate functional testing? It helps a lot. Low-code and record-and-playback tools exist and can get you started, but suites written in code are easier to review, version and maintain once they grow past a few dozen tests. Which framework should I use? Use whatever fits your stack. For APIs, your language's standard test runner plus an HTTP client is enough. For browsers, Playwright and Cypress are both solid choices. The habits in this post matter far more than the framework. How long does it take to automate functional testing? A first useful set, say ten API tests and two UI tests running in CI, is usually a few days of focused work. Getting to a suite the whole team trusts takes months, mostly because of data, flakiness and ownership rather than writing tests. Wrapping up Automating functional testing comes down to a short loop: choose what matters, test it where it lives, control the data, and let CI run it every time. Start with five tests, not five hundred. Get them green, keep them green, and add more each time something breaks. That's slower than it sounds on paper, and it works.

title: How We Built a Free 3D Meeting Room Camera & Mic Coverage Visualiser for Corporate AV Planning
summary: A meeting room can look well equipped and still leave someone outside the camera frame. A microphone symbol in the middle of a floor plan says little about whether the person at the far end of the table will be heard. The Kasturi 3D Meeting Room Visualiser lets a planner check those positions before discussing a room design. Change the room, seats, screen and video bar; the floor plan, 3D view, camera view and coverage status follow the same configuration. Planning is free. Downloading a PDF asks for a name, company and work email, and the page explains the engineering follow-up. Start with one room state The served application uses a JavaScript room state for dimensions, seats, table layout, screen and device selection. A shared state matters because the camera view and the floor plan must describe the same room. A planner should not see a covered seat in one view and an old layout in another. The live source loads Three.js for the 3D scene and jsPDF for the export. The useful design choice is the common room model: the geometry and equipment list can be rebuilt from the same inputs. This article describes the observable implementation; it does not claim a complete source-code audit or real-device compatibility test. Camera coverage is geometry with limits For a horizontal field of view θ, the ideal cone width at perpendicular distance d is: coverage width = 2 × d × tan(θ / 2) Each seat also needs to sit in front of the camera and within usable reach. A 90-degree camera gives an ideal 6 m span at a perpendicular distance of 3 m. That calculation alone says nothing about whether the far participant's face is large enough, whether another participant blocks the view, or how auto-framing will behave. The live page identifies manufacturer sources and its assumptions, including cases where camera reach is inferred from microphone range. Those inferred values need to stay distinguishable from published specifications. Microphone circles need an explanation A floor-plan pickup circle is a first check. Its radius does not model glass reflections, HVAC noise, speaker level, microphone directivity or how far-end speech reaches the AEC reference. The visualiser lists Neat, Yealink, HP Poly, Logitech, Jabra and Cisco. Some ranges are inferred from certified room dimensions, and some expansion-microphone ranges are marked as unverified in the served code. Model-specific claims should be checked against the current manufacturer document before purchase. For a glass-walled boardroom, move from geometric planning to room assessment: microphone placement, acoustic treatment, loudspeaker layout and DSP configuration work together. AEC does not replace acoustic treatment. Keep exports useful to the next person The live tool offers a three-page plan with the floor plan and seat checks, 3D and camera views, and equipment list. A copyable room link makes the discussion repeatable. Both are planning references; the page says the final design needs a site survey. The export form sends details for follow-up. This is a disclosed lead flow, so the tool should not be described as an anonymous or entirely ungated PDF download. What a browser plan can settle It can expose a chair outside an ideal camera angle, a long room that needs another audio strategy, or a screen that deserves a readability check. It cannot establish intelligibility, certify a room system or replace commissioning. Try the room visualiser , develop the brief in the room designer , explore our open-source MIT Malaysia meeting-room AV planning reference on GitHub , or review Kasturi's Malaysia AV starting budgets . Kasturi Technology Sdn. Bhd. is based in Petaling Jaya, Malaysia.

title: Secure Next.js Server Actions for Remotion-Based AI Video Generation
summary: Secure Next.js Server Actions for Remotion-Based AI Video Generation The page hits at 3:07 a.m.: the promo renderer has burned the monthly model quota, and the key that belonged on the server is inside a client chunk. I was not on the video-shotcraft team. I was the external architect asked to integrate Vincentwei1021/video-shotcraft into a Next.js 15 app without turning Remotion previews into a credential leak. The repo already does the creative work—124 shot recipe cards, 150 motion previews, beat-synced audio, sound design, and a Motion Workbench export into JianYing (CapCut CN). Remotion owns the pixels. The outage lives in the boundary around them. What fails in production is not the composition. A misplaced 'use client' around shot generation inlines process.env.AI_API_KEY into the browser bundle, visible to bundle analysis or the network panel. Moving that fetch entirely client-side to “fix” the leak buys a request waterfall that wrecks LCP, because the browser cannot prioritize assets the server never rendered. The mistake is treating the preview as a pure client island instead of a server pipeline: validate input, gate the session, call the model, then hand a shot id to Remotion. Server Action: validate, gate, then call The action below is the only place the relay credential may exist. Zod rejects a short or illegal shot payload before any network hop. getServerSession runs before the fetch. Failures return a discriminated union— VALIDATION_ERROR , AUTH_ERROR , or API_ERROR —so the UI can branch without stack traces, upstream URLs, or the bearer token. Operational boundary: pass a real auth provider into getServerSession . Treat any non-OK relay response as terminal for that attempt. Do not hide a retry loop inside the request the user is watching; retries belong in a budgeted queue. Recovery is explicit. The caller renders the typed error. revalidatePath('/promos') runs only after a shot id returns. // app/actions/generateShot.ts 'use server' ; import { z } from 'zod' ; import { getServerSession } from 'next-auth' ; // replace with your auth provider import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache' ; const schema = z . object ( { prompt : z . string ( ) . min ( 10 , 'Prompt must be at least 10 characters long' ) , style : z . enum ( [ 'cinematic' , 'minimal' , 'product' ] ) . optional ( ) , aspectRatio : z . enum ( [ '16:9' , '1:1' ] ) . default ( '16:9' ) , } ) ; export type GenerateShotError = | { message : string ; code : 'VALIDATION_ERROR' } | { message : string ; code : 'AUTH_ERROR' } | { message : string ; code : 'API_ERROR' } ; export async function generateShot ( formData : FormData ) : Promise < | { success : true ; shotId : string } | { success : false ; error : GenerateShotError } > { try { const session = await getServerSession ( ) ; if ( ! session ? . user ) { throw new Error ( 'Unauthorized access' ) ; } const rawInput = { prompt : formData . get ( 'prompt' ) , style : formData . get ( 'style' ) , aspectRatio : formData . get ( 'aspectRatio' ) , } ; const validated = schema . parse ( rawInput ) ; // AI relay call – keep secrets server-side const aiResponse = await fetch ( 'https://b-lost.com/v1/video-generate' , { method : 'POST' , headers : { 'Content-Type' : 'application/json' , Authorization : `Bearer ${process.env.AI_API_KEY}` , } , body : JSON . stringify ( { prompt : validated . prompt , style : validated . style , aspectRatio : validated . aspectRatio , } ) , } ) ; if ( ! aiResponse . ok ) { throw new Error ( `AI service returned ${aiResponse.status}` ) ; } const { shotId } = await aiResponse . json ( ) ; revalidatePath ( '/promos' ) ; return { success : true , shotId } ; } catch ( err ) { if ( err instanceof z . ZodError ) { return { success : false , error : { message : err . errors [ 0 ] . message , code : 'VALIDATION_ERROR' } , } ; } if ( err instanceof Error && err . message . includes ( 'Unauthorized' ) ) { return { success : false , error : { message : err . message , code : 'AUTH_ERROR' } } ; } return { success : false , error : { message : 'Failed to generate shot' , code : 'API_ERROR' } , } ; } } Schema first, session second, relay third. The union is the only contract the client may depend on. Stream the preview, do not block the shell Remotion’s <Player> is heavy. The Server Component keeps the shell honest: Suspense paints a skeleton immediately, and PreviewContent suspends until the action returns a shot id. A thrown error must hit an error boundary you own, not stringify internals into the DOM. One constraint: the platform FormData constructor does not accept a plain object. Build FormData in the client submit handler, or pass a typed object straight into the action, and let this component receive already-checked props. The sample shows the streaming shape. Do not ship new FormData({ prompt }) as a runtime recipe. // components/VideoPreview.tsx import { Suspense } from 'react' ; import { Player } from '@remotion/player' ; import { generateShot } from '@/actions/generateShot' ; import RemotionComposition from './RemotionComposition' ; async function PreviewContent ( { prompt } : { prompt : string } ) { const result = await generateShot ( new FormData ( { prompt } ) ) ; // FormData from client if ( ! result . success ) { throw new Error ( result . error . message ) ; } return ( < Player component = { RemotionComposition } compositionWidth = { 1280 } compositionHeight = { 720 } durationInFrames = { 240 } fps = { 30 } style = { { width : '100%' , maxWidth : '640px' } } inputProps = { { shotId : result . shotId } } /> ) ; } export default function VideoPreview ( { prompt } : { prompt : string } ) { return ( < Suspense fallback = { < div className = "skeleton-loader h-96 w-full animate-pulse rounded-xl bg-zinc-100" /> } > < PreviewContent prompt = { prompt } /> </ Suspense > ) ; } That boundary is what keeps variable model latency from freezing the rest of the promo editor. The skeleton is the product during a cold start near 280 ms, not a placeholder you delete later. Wiring Next.js to Remotion Next.js 15 enables Server Actions by default; the experimental flag is documentary, not a feature unlock. The webpack alias is a safety rail when resolution gets confused between the app and the Remotion entry. Keep FPS, entry, and beat-sync defaults in remotion.config.ts so they are not scattered through client components. // next.config.js module . exports = { experimental : { serverActions : true , // default in Next.js 15 } , webpack : ( config ) => { // Optional: force Remotion to resolve correctly config . resolve . alias = { . . . config . resolve . alias , '@remotion/player' : '@remotion/player' , } ; return config ; } , } ; // remotion.config.ts import { Config } from '@remotion/cli' ; export default Config ( { // 150 motion previews per promo defaultProps : { beatSync : true , } , // Server-side rendering stays in Next.js entry : './src/RemotionEntry.tsx' , } ) ; The dilemma I will not paper over Moving Zod and the relay onto the server removes the client secret and, in the benchmarks I ran while integrating this repo, improved LCP by roughly 35–45 percent. You pay with one hop per shot and a cold start around 280 ms against the B-Lost relay at https://b-lost.com/v1 . One hundred twenty-four separate actions recreate the waterfall you just removed. Batch prompts into one server action that accepts an array, and cache finished promos with ISR or on-demand revalidation so Remotion’s memory cost is paid only when a prompt changes. Batching is the hard call. It is faster and cheaper until one bad prompt fails the array, and you must decide whether a partial promo is shippable or whether you fail closed and discard the batch. I have watched teams hide that choice behind retries until the quota page fires again. How do you fail a 124-shot batch when shot 37 is poison—abort the promo, or commit the other 123 and leave a hole the editor has to see?

title: [Gemini in Action] Dev.to Text & Image Translator: Redrawing Chinese Screenshots with Nano Banana Pro & Gemini 4 Neon as Judge
summary: Background My workflow for writing technical articles is: first write in Chinese on my own blog, push a draft to Dev.to, and finally use a small tool I wrote, devto-blog-translation-tool , to translate all Chinese drafts into English and publish them in one go. I've been using this tool for a while. Text translation has always been solid, but one flaw has become increasingly obvious: The article is translated into English, but the screenshots inside are still full of Chinese. For example, in my recent Kalamos Devlog series, every post has several app screenshots and architecture diagrams. English readers ended up seeing English text paired with Chinese images, which felt very jarring. So this time I added a new feature: when translating an article, if Chinese text is detected in an image, ask Gemini to redraw an English version and swap out the image in the post. As usual, the entire feature was built inside Herdr: Claude Code handled writing specs and reviews, while Antigravity (agy, powered by Gemini 4 Neon) in the right pane wrote the code, going through six rounds of "implementation → review → real-world testing". However, the star of this post isn't the workflow—it's just how good Gemini itself is at "translating images" and "translating long-form articles" . 1. What the Entire Pipeline Looks Like Before translating the body text of each Chinese article, it first runs through an image processing pass: Extract Image URLs ─▶ Download ─▶ Detect Chinese + Estimate Char Count ─▶ Redraw in English ─▶ Compare & Verify (Original vs. New) ─▶ Upload to GCS & Replace URLs Step Model Used What It Does Detect Chinese Gemini 4 Neon ( gemini-4-neon ) Inspects the image to determine if it contains Chinese and estimates roughly how many Chinese characters there are Redraw in English Nano Banana Pro ( gemini-3-pro-image ) Takes the original image and outputs a new image with the same layout, color scheme, and icons, replacing only the text with English (2K, automatically choosing the aspect ratio closest to the original) Compare & Verify Gemini 4 Neon Looks at both the original and new images together to confirm there is no leftover Chinese and no missing panels or information Translate Content & Title Gemini 4 Neon Translates the entire markdown; if the title exceeds Dev.to's 128-character limit, rewrites and shortens it automatically The new image is uploaded to a publicly readable Google Cloud Storage bucket, and the image URL in the article is replaced with the GCS URL. If any image fails at any step, it simply logs a warning and keeps the original image without failing the entire article. The prompt for redrawing the image is actually quite simple: Recreate this image exactly, keeping layout, style, colors, icons and non-text content identical, but translate all Chinese text into natural English. Keep code, URLs, and proper nouns as-is. What truly surprised me is how much Nano Banana Pro can accomplish with just this one prompt. 2. Where Gemini Shines at Translating Images 1. Near 1-to-1 Redraws of UI Screenshots Here is the update dialog that pops up when Kalamos detects a new version. The original is in Chinese: After handing it to Nano Banana Pro: A few details that I think it nailed: Layout, rounded corners, color scheme, and button colors are completely preserved —at first glance, you'd think it's a screenshot of a native English UI from the app. Buttons use idiomatic software UI phrasing : "稍後 / 立即更新" is translated as "Later / Update Now", rather than a stiff literal translation. The version number 0.8.0 → 0.8.1 and arrow symbol are kept as-is , and English headings like Patch Changes are left untouched. The original image was only 948×612, while the output is 2K resolution , making it even sharper than the original. 2. It Understands What the Screen Is Saying, Not Just Swapping Words The YAML document information preview at the beginning of this article is the one I find most impressive: Not only did it translate "文件資訊" into "Document Information" and tags like 技術寫作 and 靜態部落格 into Technical Writing and Static Blog , it also translated the article body and blockquote into fluent English—while keeping the body text in a serif font and preserving the green border on the left side of the blockquote . What really made me smile was the bottom right corner: the original " 183 字 " was changed to " 183 Words ". This means the model understood it's an editor's word count, and that an English UI should display "words" rather than literally translating "字" into "characters". At the same time, YAML keys like title , date , author , and draft , as well as values like 2026-11-24 , Evan Lin , Maintainer , and false , were all left completely untouched. It clearly distinguishes between UI text that should be translated and data that must not be modified. Of course, it's not flawless: if you look closely at the last line of the blockquote, there's a repeated word "exactly exactly". Small typos like this even slipped past the subsequent verification step—it's the kind of minor imperfection you currently have to accept with image translation. 3. Gemini 4 Neon as the Judge: Catching Images That Are "Wrong Without Any Chinese" Image generation is inherently stochastic. For the Quick Open panel (Cmd+P) screenshot, the first redraw attempt came out like this: All the text was indeed translated into English, but the entire search panel vanished , leaving only the article content behind it. That panel was the whole point of the screenshot—swapping it in like this would actually mislead readers. At the time, my verification only checked "is there any Chinese left?", so it slipped through. Later, I changed it to pass both the original and new images to Gemini 4 Neon for comparison : The first image is the original image, and the second image is its English-translated version. ... Does the second image preserve all major UI elements, panels, dialogs, chart/diagram sections, and information from the first image? ... Testing with the exact same failed image, Neon pinpointed the issue immediately: The central quick-open search dialog modal from the original image is completely missing. Meanwhile, for the other two good images, it reported preserves_content: true . When I ran it for real later, the regenerated version kept the panel completely intact and passed verification: Notice how the green fuzzy-match highlights ( k , a , l , m ) in the filename list are still in the right positions, the "最近" badge became "Recent", and the bottom shortcut hints "↑↓ 移動 Enter 開啟 ⌘Enter 新分頁 Esc 關閉" were translated into "↑↓ Move Enter Open ⌘Enter New Tab Esc Close". Using one Gemini to draw the image and another Gemini to inspect and gatekeep it —this combination was the most worthwhile design decision of the whole project. 4. Estimating Character Count: Knowing Which Images Not to Touch Not every image is suitable for redrawing. The first version had no guardrails, and when I tried it on a Windows architecture diagram (2880×2570, packed densely with Chinese text), the result was rough: Only the title and left-column labels were translated into English; the two large middle sections remained in Chinese, with glyphs distorted into nonexistent garbled characters The English had typos like Portripring Ads and macos-teest The output was only 1094×976 (at the time I hadn't specified a resolution, so it defaulted to 1K) That image had actually already been swapped in on Dev.to—I reverted it to the original as soon as I noticed. The solution was to have the detection step also estimate how many Chinese characters are in the image , and if it exceeds a threshold, skip it and keep the original. Gemini 4 Neon's estimates turned out to be very useful: Image Est. Chinese Chars Result Auto-update trust chain flowchart ~710 Skipped, kept original Windows cross-platform architecture diagram ~533 Skipped, kept original External PR review flowchart ~390 Skipped, kept original Side-by-side Chinese/English UI comparison ~221 Skipped, kept original YAML document information preview ~127 ✅ Redrawn Cmd+P Quick Open ~115 ✅ Redrawn Update dialog ~92 ✅ Redrawn I currently set the threshold at 150: regular UI screenshots are handed to Gemini to redraw, while information-dense architecture diagrams are safely kept as-is. 3. Where Gemini Shines at Translating Long Articles The images are eye-catching, but translating the article body itself is what I actually rely on day to day. After switching to Gemini 4 Neon, several aspects of its performance really put my mind at ease. 1. Translating 18,000 Characters in a Single Pass Feature Evolution After Open-Sourcing is the longest post in the series: Metric Value Original length 17,810 characters Chinese character count 6,418 Output tokens 9,255 Thinking tokens 3,052 Time taken ~115 seconds The entire markdown file was sent in one shot and translated in a single pass, preserving all heading levels, tables, code blocks, and links. The resulting English body was about 37,000 characters, using only about one-fifth of the output limit (65,536). 2. Knowing When to Preserve Intentionally Quoted Chinese After translating, I checked the output and found 21 Chinese characters remaining in the body. At first I thought it missed them, but on closer inspection, every single one was supposed to stay : When the article mentioned an error message expected on screen in an E2E test, it preserved the original Chinese string and added an English explanation: When the article introduced the changeset guidelines, explaining that the format must be written in Traditional Chinese as **標題** ：說明 , it also preserved this example: If those two places had been translated into English, the article would actually become factually wrong. It understands that this Chinese text is the "subject being discussed" rather than "content to be translated" —that's far smarter than naive machine translation. In addition, image alt text was translated along with the rest, for example: Real dialog appearing during a real-machine update check for Kalamos v0.8.0 on macOS: showing current version 0.8.0 → new version 0.8.1 and CHANGELOG content For readers using screen readers, this is also a very important detail. 3. Automatically Rewriting Titles That Are Too Long Dev.to has a 128-character limit for titles, and my Chinese titles often blow past that once translated into English. My old approach was hard truncation, which resulted in titles like this: …Using Multiple Agents to Review and Take Over Exte Now I ask Gemini 4 Neon to rewrite it within 128 characters. Testing the same 150-character title twice: 120 characters : [Kalamos Devlog] After Open-Sourcing: Feature Evolution (v0.2 to v0.7) and Multi-Agent Review & Takeover of External PRs 126 characters : [Kalamos Devlog] After Open-Sourcing: v0.2–v0.7 Feature Evolution & Using Multiple Agents to Review and Take Over External PRs The leading [Kalamos Devlog] tag is preserved, none of the key information is lost, and it reads far more naturally than a hard cut. Only if both rewrite attempts fail does it fall back to "truncating at a word boundary". 4. A Few Pitfalls Hit During Implementation For anyone else looking to build something similar with Gemini: The new Go SDK defaults to API v1, but these models are only available in v1beta. On the very first real run, google.golang.org/genai returned models/gemini-3-flash-preview is not found for API version v1 . All my unit tests used mocks, so they completely missed this. The fix is to pass HTTPOptions: genai.HTTPOptions{APIVersion: "v1beta"} when creating the client. Thinking tokens in reasoning models count toward MaxOutputTokens . Title shortening was originally set to 4096, and Gemini 4 Neon burned through the entire budget just thinking, failing both times. Bumping it to 16384 made it rock solid—and you're only billed for actual usage anyway. Long articles occasionally "overthink". The first time I translated that long post, it hit the limit and failed, yet re-testing via the API used only one-fifth of the limit—seeming like an occasional runaway thinking loop. After adding an "auto-retry once on hitting the limit", re-running that post succeeded on the first try. Always run post-generation verification, and compare against the original image. Checking only "is there any Chinese?" isn't enough—image models can accidentally omit critical elements. Having another model inspect it side by side with the original is the only way to catch these mistakes. 5. How to Use It The tool is open-source: kkdai/devto-blog-translation-tool . Image translation is an optional feature—if GCS_BUCKET isn't set, it behaves exactly as before. # 1. Allow the program to upload images using your GCP credentials gcloud auth application-default login # 2. Create a publicly readable bucket gcloud storage buckets create gs://YOUR_BUCKET --uniform-bucket-level-access gcloud storage buckets add-iam-policy-binding gs://YOUR_BUCKET \ --member=allUsers --role=roles/storage.objectViewer # 3. Set environment variables (can also be placed in .env) export GCS_BUCKET = YOUR_BUCKET export IMAGE_MAX_CHINESE_CHARS = 150 # Default is 60; increase if you have many UI screenshots # 4. Run go build -o translator ./cmd/translator && ./translator When it runs, you'll see the processing result for each image: 🖼️ Image 1/4: .../kalamos-dev-collab-pr-workflow.png ... ⏭️ too much text (~390 Chinese chars), keeping original 🖼️ Image 2/4: .../kalamos-dev-collab-quick-open.png ... ✅ replaced 🖼️ Image 3/4: .../kalamos-dev-collab-front-matter.png ... ✅ replaced 🖼️ Image 4/4: .../kalamos-dev-collab-bilingual.png ... ⏭️ too much text (~228 Chinese chars), keeping original Translating content... (removing frontmatter) ✅ Updating article ID 5118206 and publishing... ✅ Published! ⚠️ Reminder: This tool translates all drafts with Chinese titles and publishes them directly , and uploaded images are stored in a public bucket. For your first run, it's recommended to keep only a single test article. Conclusion My biggest takeaway this time is: Gemini's image models are already good enough for "localization" . As long as it's a standard UI screenshot, the English version redrawn by Nano Banana Pro is high enough quality to go straight into a published article. However, it's not a silver bullet. Architecture diagrams packed with dense text still break, and generation results vary from run to run. So what actually made this feature production-ready wasn't how powerful a single model is, but these three lines of defense: Estimate character count first , avoiding images it can't draw well; Compare and verify against the original image , letting Gemini 4 Neon act as the judge; Keep the original on any failure —better to leave an image unchanged than swap in a broken one. Now, in the English edition of my Kalamos Devlog series, the UI screenshots—the update dialog, Quick Open, and YAML preview—have all been replaced with English versions, while the dense architecture diagrams remain untouched. From now on, when writing new posts, I just need to focus on writing in Chinese and leave the rest to Gemini.

title: Tripo3D or GenAnywhere? What I Learned Splitting a Site From Its Objects
summary: The question I keep getting is which of these two AI tools to use. After a month on a drive-in revival, my answer is that they do not overlap enough to compete. One models land, one models stuff, and the only decision that matters is where the land ends. Here is how that worked on a real job, with numbers. The brief An eight-and-a-half-acre drive-in, closed since 1994, reopening as a movie lot plus a weekend flea market. For a zoning hearing: six renders and one 1:300 model. Constraints: four weeks, a 1991 survey with hand notes, an uninspected screen tower, and a client family in the room. The rule I used If it appears on a tax map, GenAnywhere. If it has a serial number, Tripo3D. Everything else is judgment. Step 1: land I drew a box on the map around the site plus a margin, about 600 by 600 feet, and let GenAnywhere generate it. • Input: one rectangle on a map. • Output: lot surface, neighboring houses, strip mall, tree line, road edge, roof shapes. • Time: under fifteen minutes. • Fidelity: right for massing, light, and sightlines. Wrong for boundaries and anything you would measure. It also invented a building in the east field and flattened the screen tower into a wall panel. Both were deleted. That is normal for a context model, and why the survey stayed open the whole time. Step 2: assets Tripo3D took three kinds of input and I used all three. • Sketch: the ticket booth, from a page of the owner's graph paper. Best result of the batch. • Photo: a speaker post from a phone picture of one still standing in row 3. • Text: picnic tables, bins, bollards, the screen tower, the playground slide. Each simple object took ten to twenty minutes. The tower took a morning, because bracing is geometry Tripo3D has to guess, and it guessed a different pattern on each side. Segmentation split the tower into screen, frame, and legs so the frame could serve a second camera. Topology optimization cut it enough that a browser viewer loads the scene without a stall. Exports mattered more than expected: GLB for the web preview, FBX for the renderer, STL for the model, OBJ for the civil engineer checking queue geometry. Step 3: merge and verify Everything went into one scene, with a person-height block and a car-sized block for scale. Then the checks. • Tower legs against the base plate from the survey: off by about eight inches. Fixed. • Lot width: three feet narrow against the survey. The site model lost that argument. • Door height on the ticket booth: right after I reset it, wrong out of the box. The lot fix is the one worth remembering. The error was invisible in the drone view and obvious to the client's son, who has parked there for years. Two triangles of mismatch cost us a day. Where the handoff broke • Units. One export arrived in centimeters and made the booth knee-high on the first merge. • Pivots. Assets land at the center of the world, centered on their bounding box, so "on the ground" is always a manual step. • Texture repetition. The speaker post texture tiled visibly once it was placed forty times, so I baked a variant. None of these are dealbreakers. All of them are invisible in a tool's marketing. Where the time went Roughly a day on the land, three days on assets, two days on merge, render, and print. The rest was meetings. Hand-modeling, the land alone would have been two days and forty speaker posts an afternoon of array and cleanup. The saving is real, but it is not in the generation. It is in not modeling context nobody will look at. What I would automate next A scale gate that compares every asset bounding box to a target dimension before it enters the scene. A naming convention that survives export, so row numbers stay attached. And a flat-material render pass, which would have caught the tower-leg mismatch a day early. The scorecard Land: GenAnywhere. Fast, plausible, good for light and massing, useless for exact boundaries. Objects: Tripo3D. Sketch input is the sleeper feature, segmentation saves hours, and the export list covers whatever comes next. The seam is still manual and still where the errors live. That is not a knock on either product, just the shape of the work.

title: CVE-2026-136716: Drupal corrige falha que mantém expostos sites com a correção anterior
summary: CVE-2026-136716: Drupal corrige falha que mantém expostos sites com a correção anterior O Drupal publicou em 25 de novembro de 2026 o aviso SA-CORE-2026-019 para a CVE-2026-136716, uma falha altamente crítica de contorno de controles de acesso. Sites em estado de instalação incompleto ou incomum podem continuar vulneráveis à tomada do site, inclusive em produção. O aviso chegou oito dias depois da correção SA-CORE-2026-017 (CVE-2026-132165), que tratava uma falha no mesmo arquivo, core/install.php, capaz de levar à tomada do site ou à execução de código. A correção anterior não protege contra a nova falha: sites que a instalaram também precisam atualizar novamente. Exploração e urgência O Drupal classifica as duas vulnerabilidades como altamente críticas: a anterior recebeu 20 de 25, e a nova, 21 de 25. O projeto informa que ambas estão sendo exploradas. Ataques contra sites em produção foram registrados a partir de 19 de novembro de 2026, às 19h UTC, pouco depois da divulgação da primeira correção. A CISA incluiu a CVE-2026-132165 em seu catálogo de vulnerabilidades exploradas em 24 de novembro e fixou 27 de novembro como prazo. A CVE-2026-136716 ainda não constava na edição de 25 de novembro, mas o Drupal já relata exploração ativa, então a ausência no catálogo não reduz a urgência. Versões afetadas e corrigidas Nas linhas com suporte, a versão indicada na última coluna corrige os dois avisos. Uma instalação abaixo desse número permanece exposta, mesmo que já tenha recebido a correção anterior. LinhaCorreção anteriorNova correçãoAtualizar para11.4.xAbaixo de 11.4.13Abaixo de 11.4.1411.4.1411.3.xAbaixo de 11.3.22Abaixo de 11.3.2311.3.2310.6.xAbaixo de 10.6.22Abaixo de 10.6.2310.6.23 As linhas 11.2, 11.1 e 11.0, assim como 10.5 e anteriores, Drupal 9 e Drupal 8, também são afetadas e estão fora de suporte. A orientação é migrar para 11.3 ou 11.4, ou para 10.6, conforme a instalação. Os números estavam corretos em 26 de novembro de 2026. Como o Drupal publicou duas atualizações de segurança para esse código em uma semana, confira o aviso SA-CORE-2026-019 e a página de segurança no dia da atualização, para identificar uma versão pontual mais recente, se houver. Confira a versão e as dependências Confira a versão instalada pela linha de comando, a partir da raiz do projeto, onde fica o arquivo composer.json. O Composer consulta o arquivo de lock, que registra as dependências implantadas, enquanto o Drush confirma a versão do site inicializado. cd /var/www/drupal composer show drupal/core | head -12 vendor/bin/drush status --fields=drupal-version,php-version,db-driver,db-status,bootstrap,root,site O comando composer outdated também compara as versões instaladas às releases permitidas pelas restrições do projeto e mostra atualizações pendentes para pacotes Drupal. composer outdated 'drupal/*' Na versão de laboratório, o Drupal 11.4.13 já corrigia o aviso anterior, mas ainda estava exposto à CVE-2026-136716. A interface administrativa não indicava essa diferença, por isso a conferência manual da versão é importante. O comando antigo drush pm:security foi removido das versões atuais do Drush. Tarefas agendadas ou rotinas de CI que ainda o executem podem falhar sem deixar claro que a consulta não foi feita; use composer audit --locked para verificar os avisos associados ao arquivo de lock. composer audit --locked Na execução de laboratório, a auditoria encontrou 18 avisos em sete pacotes, incluindo drupal/core, Symfony e Twig. As dependências também precisam ser consideradas na atualização; incluir a auditoria no pipeline de implantação permite detectar novos avisos quando forem publicados. Bloqueie o instalador no servidor web Segundo o aviso do Drupal, um instalador já protegido não fica vulnerável a essa falha. Em produção, o arquivo não é necessário depois da instalação; para implantar sites novos, o comando drush site:install evita o instalador pelo navegador. Faça o bloqueio antes de seguir para a investigação e a atualização. No Nginx, localize o bloco de servidor correto com sudo nginx -T e insira a regra antes da configuração de PHP. O prefixo ^~ também cobre caminhos que continuem depois de /core/install.php. location ^~ /core/install.php { return 404; } Teste a configuração e verifique a rota principal, a alternativa e um caminho com sufixo. A regra precisa estar nos blocos que atendem HTTP ou HTTPS, conforme a configuração do site. sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx curl -I http://example.com/core/install.php curl -IL http://example.com/install.php curl -I http://example.com/core/install.php/foo Na configuração de laboratório, as três rotas responderam com 404. Respostas 403 ou 404 indicam bloqueio; um 200 exige revisar o bloco de servidor e a ordem das regras. Repita os testes de fora do servidor para verificar possíveis rotas ou respostas de CDN e balanceadores. No Apache, inclua a restrição no host virtual. A diretiva em .htaccess pode causar erro 500. O exemplo abaixo bloqueia o acesso à rota e também aos caminhos que começam com ela. Require all denied sudo apachectl configtest && sudo systemctl reload apache2 O teste de laboratório retornou 403 para o instalador; a rota /install.php redirecionou para a rota bloqueada. No RHEL, o serviço Apache se chama httpd. Em hospedagem compartilhada sem acesso ao host virtual, o guia do Drupal descreve uma regra em .htaccess. Investigue antes de atualizar o banco Antes de executar drush updb, verifique se houve tomada do site. A atualização do banco reescreve valores que podem ajudar a identificar uma invasão anterior. A ordem recomendada é bloquear o instalador, investigar sinais de comprometimento e só então atualizar o banco. Evite entrar como usuário 1 antes de conferir o horário de login desse usuário: o acesso pode sobrescrever justamente o valor que será auditado. A página de verificação de comprometimento do Drupal orienta essa etapa antes da atualização. Atualize e mantenha o bloqueio Depois das verificações, atualize o Drupal para a versão corrigida de sua linha e execute a atualização de banco. A atualização pelo Composer fecha os dois avisos nas linhas compatíveis, mas a etapa de banco com Drush também é necessária. drush updb O Drupal recomenda remover também web/core/install.php após cada instalação e atualização do Composer, junto do bloqueio no servidor. Os comandos abaixo configuram essa remoção para os dois eventos e executam uma instalação de dependências. composer config scripts.post-install-cmd 'rm -f web/core/install.php' composer config scripts.post-update-cmd 'rm -f web/core/install.php' composer install Antes de usar composer config, confira os scripts existentes: o comando substitui o evento e pode apagar rotinas já configuradas, como as do modelo drupal-composer/drupal-project. Nesse caso, acrescente a remoção à lista existente em composer.json. Ajuste também o caminho se a raiz pública do projeto não for web/; projetos antigos podem usar docroot/ ou a própria raiz. Como composer install --no-scripts pula a remoção, mantenha o bloqueio do servidor web ativo. Consulte o guia de atualização e verificação do Drupal para os procedimentos relacionados. Confira mais em: https://guiadeti.com.br/noticias/drupal-cve-2026-136716-falha-critica-instalador/
