title: How You Can Run Massive LLMs Even on Consumer Hardware (5 Bottlenecks, Simple Fixes & Step-by-Step Code)
summary: You see an exciting new 35B or 300B+ open-source AI model drop on HuggingFace. You open your laptop, your gaming PC with an 8 GB–16 GB GPU, or a free Google Colab T4, run AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...) —and within seconds your terminal explodes with: RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Or worse, your system RAM hits 100%, swap kicks in, and your entire computer freezes before generating a single word. Most people assume you need $30,000 enterprise GPUs to run big Large Language Models. You don't. Running a massive modern LLM on consumer hardware isn't blocked by one impossible wall—it's blocked by 5 small, surprisingly simple software mistakes that standard loaders make by default. In this guide, we'll break down each of those 5 small bottlenecks one by one: The Simple Problem (in plain English + 1-line math) The Simple Fix (how to rethink it) Step-by-Step Python Code (clean, readable code showing exactly how it works) At the end, you'll also see how to run all of this out-of-the-box in 3 commands —running a 35-Billion-parameter model inside 2.7 GB of GPU VRAM at 30 tokens/sec (or 43 tokens/sec on a 15 GB T4), and even a 306-Billion-parameter model on a single GPU. Bottleneck 1: Python Crashes Before Reading Any Weights The Simple Problem When you initialize a PyTorch model the normal way ( model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_config(config) ), PyTorch immediately allocates random 32-bit numbers in your RAM for every single parameter before it even opens your downloaded weights file. The Math: 35 Billion parameters × 4 bytes (float32) = 140 GB of useless random numbers! Even a 32 GB PC crashes before loading byte #1 from disk. The Simple Fix Build the model on PyTorch's "meta" device first. A meta model is just an empty architectural blueprint—it knows every layer's shape and connections, while using literally 0 bytes of RAM and 0 bytes of GPU VRAM . Then you stream real 4-bit or 16-bit weights into it piece by piece. Step-by-Step Code import torch from transformers import AutoConfig , AutoModelForCausalLM def create_zero_ram_skeleton ( model_id : str ) : # Step 1: Download ONLY the tiny JSON config (~5 KB), not the 70 GB weights config = AutoConfig . from_pretrained ( model_id , trust_remote_code = True ) # Step 2: Build the entire neural network inside PyTorch's "meta" device. # Memory used on CPU RAM = 0 bytes! Memory used on GPU VRAM = 0 bytes! with torch . device ( "meta" ) : model = AutoModelForCausalLM . from_config ( config , dtype = torch . float16 , # Keep default blueprint in 16-bit, NOT 32-bit! trust_remote_code = True , ) return model Why this works: Instead of needing 140 GB of upfront scratch RAM just to construct the Python object, create_zero_ram_skeleton() finishes in milliseconds using 0 MB . Bottleneck 2: Your Vocabulary Table Wastes 1–2 GB of GPU VRAM The Simple Problem Modern 2026 LLMs support 150,000 to 250,000 tokens (words/subwords across dozens of languages and code). If vocab_size = 248,320 and hidden_size = 4,096 , that first lookup table ( embed_tokens ) takes: The Math: 248,320 × 4,096 × 2 bytes (FP16) ≈ 2.03 GB of GPU VRAM! The Irony: To generate the next word, the GPU only looks up 1 single row ( 8 KB ) out of those 248,320 rows! Keeping 2 GB parked on a 6 GB or 8 GB GPU just to read 8 KB per token is pure waste. The Simple Fix Keep embed_tokens.bin on disk/RAM using operating-system memory mapping ( mmap ) . Let the CPU grab just the 8 KB row for the current token ID and copy only those 8 KB to the GPU. GPU VRAM used = 0 MB . Step-by-Step Code import mmap import numpy as np import torch import torch . nn as nn class ZeroVramMmapEmbedding ( nn . Module ) : def __init__ ( self , bin_path : str , vocab_size : int , hidden_size : int , device : str = "cuda" ) : super ( ) . __init__ ( ) self . device = device # Step 1: Open the raw FP16 embedding file WITHOUT loading it into RAM self . _file = open ( bin_path , "rb" ) self . _mmap = mmap . mmap ( self . _file . fileno ( ) , 0 , access = mmap . ACCESS_READ ) # Step 2: Wrap the mmap buffer as a zero-copy 2D NumPy view [vocab_size, hidden_size] self . table = np . frombuffer ( self . _mmap , dtype = np . float16 , count = vocab_size * hidden_size ) . reshape ( vocab_size , hidden_size ) def forward ( self , input_ids : torch . Tensor ) -> torch . Tensor : # Step 3: Pull token IDs to CPU (usually just 1 integer during generation!) ids_cpu = input_ids . detach ( ) . cpu ( ) . numpy ( ) # Step 4: Slice ONLY the needed 8 KB row(s) and send that tiny slice to the GPU rows = np . ascontiguousarray ( self . table [ ids_cpu ] ) return torch . from_numpy ( rows ) . to ( self . device , non_blocking = True ) Result: You instantly save 1 GB to 2 GB of GPU VRAM with virtually zero speed penalty ( 8 KB takes < 0.002 ms to copy). Bottleneck 3: Loading All "Experts" When Each Word Uses Only 3% The Simple Problem Almost every frontier open model today ( Qwen3.6 , DeepSeek-V3/V4 , GLM-5 , Llama-4 , Mixtral ) uses Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) . Think of an MoE model like a hospital with 256 specialist doctors ("experts") on every floor, where each patient (token) only visits 8 doctors ( 3.1% ) : A 35B model ( Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ) only activates 3B parameters per word! Yet standard tools try to load all 256 experts onto your GPU—or offload entire floors to the CPU ( llama.cpp --n-cpu-moe ), leaving half your GPU sitting idle or crashing with OOM on 288-expert models. The Simple Fix Instead of keeping all 256 experts in a layer or zero experts in a layer, give every layer a small "VIP Parking Lot" ( Slot Arena ) in GPU VRAM—say 16 or 32 slots per layer. In natural human language (or Python code), a small group of popular experts gets picked over and over again . Tracking popularity with a simple frequency counter ( TinyLFU ) lets just 25%–50% of slots answer 70% to 88% of expert lookups directly on the GPU! Step-by-Step Code class LayerSlotCache : """Tracks which experts live inside a fixed-size GPU VRAM slot arena.""" def __init__ ( self , num_slots : int , num_experts : int ) : # Step 1: Map expert_id -> gpu_slot (-1 means NOT currently on GPU) self . expert_to_slot = [ - 1 ] * num_experts self . slot_to_expert = [ - 1 ] * num_slots # Step 2: Count how often each expert is actually requested by the router self . freq = [ 0 ] * num_experts def split_hits_and_misses ( self , selected_experts : list [ int ] ) : gpu_hits , cpu_misses = [ ] , [ ] for eid in selected_experts : self . freq [ eid ] += 1 # Step 3: Record popularity slot = self . expert_to_slot [ eid ] if slot != - 1 : gpu_hits . append ( ( eid , slot ) ) # Fast path: already in GPU VRAM! else : cpu_misses . append ( eid ) # Cold path: not in VRAM right now return gpu_hits , cpu_misses def maybe_promote ( self , cold_eid : int ) -> int | None : # Step 4: Find the least-used expert currently parked on the GPU victim_slot = min ( range ( len ( self . slot_to_expert ) ) , key = lambda s : self . freq [ self . slot_to_expert [ s ] ] if self . slot_to_expert [ s ] != - 1 else - 1 , ) resident_eid = self . slot_to_expert [ victim_slot ] # Step 5: Only replace it if the new expert is strictly MORE popular! if resident_eid == - 1 or self . freq [ cold_eid ] > self . freq [ resident_eid ] : if resident_eid != - 1 : self . expert_to_slot [ resident_eid ] = - 1 self . slot_to_expert [ victim_slot ] = cold_eid self . expert_to_slot [ cold_eid ] = victim_slot return victim_slot return None Why this works: Random one-off experts don't kick out your hot coding/conversation experts. Your GPU VRAM usage stays 100% flat and predictable —whether you give it 2.7 GB ( 8 slots/layer) or 12 GB ( 159 slots/layer). Bottleneck 4: The PCIe Cable Traffic Jam ( 8 KB vs 13.5 MB !) The Simple Problem Here is the biggest trap people fall into when building "weight streaming" engines: "Whenever a needed expert isn't in GPU VRAM, I'll just copy its weights from CPU RAM to GPU VRAM, run it, and move on!" Let's check the math over a normal PCIe cable ( ~12–16 GB/s real-world speed): 1 single large expert's weights (4-bit): ~2 MB to 13.5 MB Across 40 layers ( 2–5 misses per layer): 200 MB to 3,000 MB copied for every single word! Your GPU spends 90% of its life stalled waiting on the PCIe cable , crawling at 2–4 tokens/sec . The Simple Fix Never move missed expert weights to the GPU during token generation. Move the tiny token vector to the CPU instead! Look at the size difference: Moving the expert weights to the GPU = 13,500 KB per miss. Moving the token hidden state to the CPU = 8 KB ( 4096 × 2 bytes )! While the GPU computes all the cached Hit experts , your multi-core CPU simultaneously multiplies that 8 KB vector against the Missed experts directly over mmap in RAM, and sends a single 8 KB result vector back to add on the GPU! GPU (VRAM Slot Arena) CPU (Multi-Core SIMD over mmap) +-----------------------------------+ +-------------------------------------+ | 1. Attention + Router | | | | 2. Send 8 KB vector + Miss IDs ---+------->| 3. Run ONLY Missed Experts in RAM | | 4. Run Cached Hit Experts on GPU | 8 KB | (Zero weight copies over PCIe!) | | 5. Final Output = GPU + CPU <-----+--------+ 4. Return 8 KB vector to GPU | +-----------------------------------+ 8 KB +-------------------------------------+ Step-by-Step Code import torch def hybrid_moe_forward ( x_gpu : torch . Tensor , # Shape: [1, hidden_size] (~8 KB in FP16) routed_ids : list [ int ] , # e.g. 8 chosen experts out of 256 routed_weights : torch . Tensor , # Router probabilities cache : LayerSlotCache , gpu_slot_arena , # Fast 4-bit GPU kernel on resident slots cpu_mmap_pool , # Parallel C++/SIMD threads over mmap file ) -> torch . Tensor : # Step 1: Split the 8 chosen experts into GPU Hits vs CPU Misses hits , misses = cache . split_hits_and_misses ( routed_ids ) # Step 2: Copy ONLY the tiny 8 KB activation vector to CPU (NOT megabytes of weights!) if misses : x_cpu = x_gpu . to ( "cpu" , non_blocking = True ) # Step 3: Launch GPU kernel for all cached Hits immediately (non-blocking) y_gpu = gpu_slot_arena . run_4bit_swiglu ( x_gpu , hits , routed_weights ) # Step 4: At the SAME TIME, CPU computes any Misses in-place over mmap if misses : y_cpu = cpu_mmap_pool . run_4bit_misses ( x_cpu , misses , routed_weights ) # Send just 8 KB back to GPU and sum the two partial answers! y_gpu = y_gpu + y_cpu . to ( x_gpu . device , non_blocking = True ) # Optional Step 5: Promote at most 1 newly hot expert in background DMA stream cache . maybe_promote ( misses [ 0 ] ) return y_gpu Result: On a 35B MoE model on an NVIDIA T4, eliminating PCIe weight stalls jumped speed from 5.3 tokens/sec -> 43.3 tokens/sec ( 8x faster) with zero loss in output quality ! Bottleneck 5: Running a 21 GB Model on a 12 GB RAM Machine (Stopping OS Double-Caching) The Simple Problem What if your quantized model is 21 GB (or 186 GB ), and your system RAM is only 12 GB (like free Colab or a budget PC)? When you read 10 GB of popular experts from your SSD via mmap and upload them into GPU VRAM, your operating system tries to be "helpful" and keeps a duplicate copy of those exact same 10 GB in system RAM (the OS file page cache). Now 10 GB of GPU VRAM + 10 GB of System RAM hold the exact same data ! Your remaining RAM runs out, and your SSD starts thrashing violently. (Bonus Linux gotcha: Python/C's standard posix_madvise(..., POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) is actually a **silent no-op * in Linux glibc —it returns 0 without freeing a single byte!)* The Simple Fix Pack each expert aligned to 16 KB OS memory pages . The exact millisecond an expert finishes copying into GPU VRAM, call the raw Linux madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) syscall on that expert's slice so the OS drops the duplicate RAM pages immediately. Now your GPU VRAM holds hot experts and your System RAM holds only non-overlapping cold experts! Step-by-Step Code import ctypes import sys MADV_DONTNEED = 4 # Linux kernel constant: "drop these clean file pages from RAM now" _libc = ctypes . CDLL ( "libc.so.6" ) if sys . platform . startswith ( "linux" ) else None def drop_duplicate_ram_pages ( mmap_base_addr : int , expert_offset : int , expert_bytes : int ) -> None : """Free Host RAM pages immediately after an expert is uploaded into GPU VRAM.""" if _libc is None : return # Step 1: Must be aligned to OS page size (4 KB on x86 Linux, 16 KB on ARM/macOS) page_addr = mmap_base_addr + expert_offset # Step 2: Call raw Linux madvise() directly (NOT glibc's no-op posix_madvise!) # Because cas_experts_q4.bin is read-only on disk, the kernel safely frees the RAM # instantly and seamlessly re-reads from NVMe only if needed later. _libc . madvise ( ctypes . c_void_p ( page_addr ) , ctypes . c_size_t ( expert_bytes ) , ctypes . c_int ( MADV_DONTNEED ) , ) Result: With disjoint RAM + VRAM residency, a 21 GB 35B model runs smoothly inside a 12 GB RAM limit at 29.1 tokens/sec , and a 186 GB 306B model runs inside a 112 GB RAM limit ( 2.1x faster than llama.cpp ) ! Try It Yourself in 3 Commands (Mac, Windows WSL2, Linux, or Colab) We combined all 5 of these techniques—plus custom 4-bit CUDA __dp4a kernels, static CUDA Graphs, C++17 AVX2 / NEON CPU pools, and native Apple Silicon Metal ( MLX ) kernels—into an open-source MIT engine: deimos-stream . # 1. Install (Apple Silicon Mac uses native Metal MLX; Linux/WSL2 uses NVIDIA CUDA) pip install -U deimos-stream # macOS (M1 / M2 / M3 / M4) pip install -U "deimos-stream[cuda]" # Linux / Windows WSL2 / Colab NVIDIA GPU # 2. Stream-convert a HuggingFace MoE model into 16KB page-aligned 4-bit format # (Try LiquidAI/LFM2.5-8B-A1B for laptops, or Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B for 6GB-16GB GPUs!) deimos-stream convert \ --model-dir Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B \ --output-dir ./qwen36_35b_q4 # 3. Chat! `--slots auto` automatically sizes the GPU slot cache to fit your free VRAM deimos-stream chat \ --store-dir ./qwen36_35b_q4 \ --backbone q4 \ --slots auto \ --tau 1.0 \ --no-verify Want to force a 35-Billion-parameter model ( 67 GB original size) into under 2.8 GB of GPU VRAM (less VRAM than a lightweight video game)? Just cap --slots 8 : deimos-stream chat --store-dir ./qwen36_35b_q4 --backbone q4 --slots 8 --tau 1.0 --no-verify Real Verified Speeds on Everyday & Single-GPU Hardware Model ( Original Size ) Hardware Tested GPU VRAM Used Generation Speed OLMoE-1B-7B ( 13.2 GB ) MacBook ( Apple Silicon Metal, Ultra-Low Mode) 0.66 GB ( 676 MiB ) 75.7 tok/s OLMoE-1B-7B ( 13.2 GB ) MacBook ( Apple Silicon Metal, --slots auto ) 3.82 GB 422.0 tok/s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ( 67.0 GB ) Single NVIDIA T4 ( --slots 8 , Ultra-Low VRAM) 2.71 GB 29.9 tok/s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ( 67.0 GB ) Single NVIDIA T4 ( --slots 64 , 8GB-Class Budget) 6.43 GB 38.8 tok/s Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ( 67.0 GB ) Single NVIDIA T4 ( --slots auto , 15GB GPU) 12.73 GB 43.3 tok/s GLM-5.3-Flash 306B ( 305.8 GB ) Single 15 GB T4 / 24 GB A10 GPU 10.7 GB / 17.0 GB 2.3 – 3.44 tok/s Key Takeaway Whenever someone tells you consumer hardware can't run modern LLMs, look at what the bytes are actually doing : Don't allocate random float32 tensors before loading ( torch.device("meta") ). Don't park 2 GB lookup tables in GPU VRAM to read 8 KB per word ( mmap ). Cache popular individual experts in a fixed VRAM arena instead of whole layers ( TinyLFU ). Never copy megabytes of missed weights over PCIe—send the 8 KB activation to the CPU instead. Drop duplicate OS page-cache copies ( madvise(MADV_DONTNEED) ) as soon as pages hit VRAM. All source code ( Python , C++17 , CUDA , and Apple MLX ) is 100% open-source (MIT) here: github.com/martianacademy/deimos-stream . If there's one specific bottleneck above—like writing your own 4-bit GPU kernel from scratch , streaming 300 GB conversions on a tiny SSD , or Apple Silicon Unified Memory zero-copy tricks —that you want a dedicated deep-dive tutorial on next, drop a comment below!

title: Discount Calculator: Why "Extra 20% Off the Sale Price" Isn't 50% Off
summary: Discount Calculator: Why "Extra 20% Off the Sale Price" Isn't 50% Off Last holiday season our small storefront ran a "30% off everything" sale and, on top of that, emailed a coupon for "an extra 20% off at checkout." Within a day, support had a pile of tickets that all said the same thing: a $120 jacket should be $60 with half off, so why did the checkout page show $67.20? The answer, of course, is that the two discounts multiply instead of add. But explaining that one-on-one, over and over, got old fast. So I wrote the math down three ways: a Python script for the team, a spreadsheet formula for support, and a browser page for anyone who just wants the number. Here's all three, plus the traps I hit along the way. The scenario The numbers from one real ticket: Jacket price: $120.00 Store sale: 30% off Coupon: extra 20% off (applied to the sale price, per the terms) Customer expected: $60.00 (30% + 20% = 50% off) Checkout showed: $67.20 $67.20 is correct. 30% off leaves 70% of the price; the extra 20% takes 80% of that . The total discount is 1 − (0.7 × 0.8) = 44%, not 50%. On a $120 jacket that's $18.80 more than the customer guessed, which is exactly the size of disappointment that turns into a ticket. Method 1: Python with Decimal (Python 3.11.1) Money in floats is asking for trouble, so I used Decimal . This is the script I ended up pasting into support replies (Python 3.11.1, standard library only): # stack_discounts.py — Python 3.11.1 from decimal import Decimal , ROUND_HALF_UP def final_price ( base : Decimal , percents : list [ Decimal ] ) -> Decimal : price = base for p in percents : price = price * ( Decimal ( "100" ) - p ) / Decimal ( "100" ) return price . quantize ( Decimal ( "0.01" ) , rounding = ROUND_HALF_UP ) base = Decimal ( "120.00" ) print ( final_price ( base , [ Decimal ( "30" ) , Decimal ( "20" ) ] ) ) # 67.20 print ( base * Decimal ( "50" ) / Decimal ( "100" ) ) # 60.00 (what the customer expected) effective = 100 - ( 100 - 30 ) * ( 100 - 20 ) / 100 print ( f "effective discount: {effective}%" ) # effective discount: 44.0% Running it prints 67.20 , 60.00 , and 44.0% . That last line became the one-liner I put in the coupon terms page. The Python decimal docs cover the rounding modes if you need banker's rounding instead of ROUND_HALF_UP . Method 2: JavaScript (Node 22.13.1) Our checkout is JavaScript, so I reproduced the same math there (Node 22.13.1): // discount.js — Node 22.13.1 const base = 120.0 ; const stacked = base * 0.7 * 0.8 ; console . log ( stacked ) ; // 67.2 console . log ( stacked . toFixed ( 2 ) ) ; // "67.20" console . log ( 100 - 0.7 * 0.8 * 100 ) ; // 44.00000000000001 Same result, one new problem: 100 - 0.7 * 0.8 * 100 comes out as 44.00000000000001 . Harmless here, but floats will bite you on prices that don't divide cleanly. A classic from our own test suite: 4.35 * 0.9 evaluates to 3.9149999999999996 , and (4.35 * 0.9).toFixed(2) returns "3.91" , not the 3.92 you'd get by rounding half up on paper. The usual fix is to work in integer cents and round once at the end, or reach for a decimal library. The toFixed docs on MDN spell out why the rounding is not what you'd expect from school math. For support staff, the plain-spreadsheet version ended up being enough: =ROUND(120 * (1 - 0.30) * (1 - 0.20), 2) → 67.20 Method 3: a browser tool when you just need the number Most of the time nobody wants a script. When a customer emails "what will I actually pay?", support opens a free online discount calculator , types in the original price and the discount, and reads off the final price and the savings. For stacked coupons you run it twice: take the first result as the new base for the second discount. It runs entirely in the browser, so there's nothing to install and nothing uploaded, which matters when the conversation involves someone's actual order. I also keep this browser-based tool pinned while writing promo copy, because it catches the "50% off!" claim before it ships instead of after. Three traps worth knowing 1. Adding percentages instead of stacking them. This is the whole ticket pile in one bullet. 30% + 20% is not 50% off; the real discount is 44%. I verified the direction the other way too: a 20% coupon followed by a 30% sale also lands on $67.20; stacking is commutative, which surprises people but follows straight from multiplication. 2. Trusting toFixed(2) to round "correctly." The 4.35 * 0.9 case above produced "3.91" where a human would write 3.92 , because the float closest to 3.915 is actually slightly below it. If your receipts must match the accountant's, compute in cents with integers: Math.round(435 * 90 / 100) gives 392 cents. Same input, different cent, real dispute. 3. Rounding per item versus at cart level. A cart with $9.99, $14.99, and $7.25 at 15% off rounds to $27.39 if you round each discounted item and sum, but $27.40 if you sum first and round once. One cent, but our payment provider rejected a settlement batch over exactly this class of mismatch. Pick one policy, write it down, and apply it everywhere. And check your jurisdiction: in some places sales tax is computed on the pre-discount price, so the receipt legitimately shows more than "price after discount" suggests. That's another source of tickets that no amount of discount math fixes. Quick summary Situation Correct math $120 base Single 30% off base × 0.70 $84.00 30% then extra 20% base × 0.70 × 0.80 $67.20 "50% off" (what customers expect) base × 0.50 $60.00 Effective stacked discount 1 − 0.70 × 0.80 44% The one-line takeaway: stacked discounts multiply, so convert each to its remainder and multiply those. Whether you do it in Python, in a spreadsheet, or in the discount calculator , do it before the coupon email goes out. Future-you in the support inbox will be grateful. More free browser-based utilities at utilvy.com.

title: Installing GDOM with a PostgreSQL Resource Library for GBase 8a
summary: GDOM (GBase Database Operation Manager), the China-domestically developed operations tool from GBASE, supports both PostgreSQL and mysql as its resource library as of 3.2B2 . This post records an install backed by an existing third-party PostgreSQL instance. From GDOM 3.7.0 onward PostgreSQL can be installed automatically, so use the bundled one if no external instance is available. The test instance was postgresql14-14.9-2PGDG.rhel7.x86_64.rpm and had to be installed beforehand . Everything below runs from the unpacked installer directory. Prerequisites Without expect the shell scripts will not run: yum install expect ./gdomSetupRPM.sh redhat7-x86_64 Supported OS types are redhat7-x86_64 , redhat8-x86_64 , kylin10-x86_64 and kylin10-aarch64 . Configuring demo.options The parameters that matter (full reference is in README.PDF inside the package): # Install directory; create it first and make sure user has access gdomRoot =/ opt / gdom gdomService = 10.0 . 2.103 # nginx sits in front, so 8080 is not the public port gdomServicePort = 8080 # Use a dedicated OS user, not an existing one user = gdom # Third-party PostgreSQL: leave gdomDb empty gdomDb = gdomDbPort = 5432 gdomDbUser = postgres gdomDbPwd = 625562 gdomDbDriver = org . postgresql . Driver # Setting gdomDbUrl overrides gdomDb. # This JDBC URL MUST NOT include a database name, or the install cannot connect. gdomDbUrl = 'jdbc:postgresql://10.0.2.103:5432/?useUnicode=true&characterEncoding=utf8&zeroDateTimeBehavior=convertToNull&allowPublicKeyRetrieval=true&useSSL=true&serverTimezone=GMT%2B8&allowMultiQueries=true' # Analysis store uses 6258 because 5258 is already taken by the local cluster gdomGBaseDb = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomGBaseDbPort = 6258 gdomGBaseDbUser = gbase2 gdomGBaseDbPwd = gbase2 gdomNginx = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomNginxPort = 8810 gdomRedis = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomRedisPort = 7481 gdomMq = 10.0 . 2.103 gdomMqPort = 9876 gdomDashBoardPort = 9898 If a database name slips into the URL, fix it afterwards in gdom/install/gdom-service/config/application.properties . Configuring mutual trust Run as root ; the script creates the OS user named by user and sets up SSH trust, prompting once for the root password and once for the gdom password: ./gdomMutualTrust.sh -a It distributes keys with ssh-copy-id . If you hit /usr/bin/ssh-copy-id: ERROR: invalid option (-f) , edit gdomTrust.exp and remove the -f flag after ssh-copy-id . Installing Move the package under the install user, fix ownership, then run the installer as that user: mv /root/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 /home/gdom/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 chown -R gdom:gdom /home/gdom/GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64 su - gdom cd GDOM-v3.2.0-build2-redhat7-x86_64/ ./gdomInstall.sh -a The installer checks ports, distributes packages, unpacks and configures middleware, then initializes the stores. Port checks: 10.0.2.103 GDOM Service 8080 available Skipped, using third-party resource library <- GDOM DB Skipped, no HaProxy 10.0.2.103 GBase 6258 available 10.0.2.103 Nginx 8810 available 10.0.2.103 Redis 7481 available 10.0.2.103 Redis 9876 available <- RocketMQ Main packages shipped: gdom-service-3.2.0.tar.gz (216 MB) ​, jdk-1.8.0_411 (140 MB) ​, gdom-agent.tar.gz (130 MB) ​, GBase8a-NoLicense-9.5.3.28.11 (61 MB) ​ and rocketmq-all-5.2.0 (144 MB) ​, plus nginx 1.27.0 and redis 6.2.7. Configuration sets gbase_8a_gbase8a.cnf to port 6258 , points the master datasource at org.postgresql.Driver , and the analysis datasource at jdbc:gbase://10.0.2.103:6258/gdom_real . Resource-library initialization is skipped because a third-party database is in use, while the analysis stores gdom_real and gdom_history get their schemas and stored procedures created automatically. Initializing the PostgreSQL database Run two scripts with psql or another client — schema first, then data (adjust names to the actual directory): psql -d gdom -f /opt/gdom/install/sql/gdom_init_pg.sql psql -d gdom -f /opt/gdom/install/sql/gdom_init_pg_data.sql The installer log names the data script gdom_init_data_pg.sql , while the distribution listing and the command above use gdom_init_pg_data.sql ; use whichever file actually exists under /opt/gdom/install/sql . Starting, accessing and stopping ./gdomStart.sh -a # GBase / Redis / Nginx / RocketMQ / GDOM Service ./gdomStop.sh -s # stop GDOM Service Once startup finishes, open http://10.0.2.103:8810 . This install ran in a VM, so an IP mapping was used. Going forward, the interesting part is the split of responsibility: GDOM still orchestrates the whole middleware stack and the gbase analysis database, and only the resource-library step is left to the DBA. Later releases are expected to automate PostgreSQL initialization and fresh PostgreSQL installation as well, which would make the external database setup optional entirely.

title: Your Grant Auditor Can Ask About Your AI Agent Years From Now. Can You Answer?
summary: A how-to for compliance-heavy European organisations that run on public money: universities, research institutes, public hospitals, municipalities, agencies, NGOs and companies in EU-funded consortia. If your organisation depends on government or EU funding, you already live with a particular kind of accountability. Every euro has conditions. Every claim needs evidence. Auditors can arrive long after the work is done, and what they find can be extended to other grants and recovered with money you may have already spent. Now add AI agents. They draft cost statements, classify expenses, answer citizens, triage applications, prepare reports and pull data from systems of record. Each of those tasks touches an obligation. And a year or three later, an auditor, a funder, a regulator or a citizen asks the same simple question: how was this decided, and can you show us? This guide explains why publicly funded organisations face that question earlier and harder than most, how to map agent work to the obligations it touches, and how to build the record that lets you answer. It closes with a 30 day plan. A note on scope. This is general information, not legal or audit advice. Funding rules differ by programme and member state, so check your grant agreement, national rules and your own legal and audit advisers. The case is an illustrative composite with invented names. Parameter names in code are illustrative. ZizkaDB records events and shows whether the record has been altered. It does not decide eligibility, make a system compliant or replace your audit function. Why funded organisations are different Four features set publicly funded bodies apart. Your costs are conditional. Funding is paid against rules on what counts as an eligible cost. If a cost is later found ineligible, it can be recovered. Under the Horizon Europe model grant agreement, beneficiaries must keep records and supporting documents to confirm proper use of funds and the costs claimed, and a published guide summarising the rules says records must be kept for five years after the final payment for grants over 60,000 euros, or three years for grants of 60,000 euros or less. A national contact point for Horizon Europe adds that the period can be longer in case of ongoing audits or national requirements. Other EU programmes and national funders have their own conditions, so check yours. Many bodies can audit you, and findings can travel. The model grant agreement includes provisions for checks, reviews and audits, including by OLAF, the European Public Prosecutor's Office and the European Court of Auditors, and a clause on the consequences of audits that deals with extension of findings. In plain terms, a weakness found in one project can prompt questions about others that used the same process. An agent that applied the same classification rule across thirty grants is one finding multiplied by thirty. Public-law rules on AI apply to you directly. The EU AI Act asks deployers of certain high-risk AI systems that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, to perform a fundamental rights impact assessment before use, and to notify the market surveillance authority of the results. Deployers of high-risk systems must also keep the logs the system generates, where under their control, for at least six months. The Digital Omnibus moved the application date for Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027, so check the final text and your timeline. Which of your systems count as high-risk depends on what they do, and that includes systems used to assess eligibility for public benefits and services. Cyber and incident rules are stricter for public bodies. Under NIS2, public administration entities of central governments are essential entities, regional ones are covered on a risk basis, and member states may extend coverage to local governments. A significant incident triggers an early warning within 24 hours, an incident notification within 72 hours and a final report within one month. If an agent is involved in an incident, you need to reconstruct what it did quickly. Add to this the usual public-sector layer: data protection law, public procurement rules, freedom of information duties in many countries, and the expectation that public money is spent transparently. The result is an organisation that is asked to prove its decisions more often than almost any other. The case: the research office and the cost classification agent This is a composite, with invented names. A university research office, call it Northfield University, uses an AI agent to prepare the cost statements for dozens of EU and national grants. The agent reads time records, invoices and payroll extracts, classifies each item against the cost categories in each grant agreement, and drafts the periodic financial report. A research accountant reviews a sample before submission. Year one. The agent classifies a recurring item, a shared equipment service contract, as a direct eligible cost for twelve projects. A prompt update in month five changes how it reads certain invoice descriptions. Staff turnover follows. The accountant who set up the review sample leaves. Year three. After final payment, a funder audit selects one of the projects. The auditor asks about the service contract cost: why was it classified as direct eligible, which version of the grant rules was applied, what evidence supported it, who verified it, and was the same treatment applied elsewhere? What Northfield has. The final report, the invoices and some application logs. The logs show the output, not the reasoning inputs. The prompt version in force that month is unclear. The reviewer has left. The agent's classification of the same item in other projects cannot be listed without re-running the whole year. What the auditor does. Finds the cost ineligible in this project, and asks whether the treatment applies to other grants. The university spends weeks reconstructing, and the answers are partly guesses. Recovery is demanded on the one project, and the finding is extended to the others. None of this requires fraud. It requires only that nobody could show how the decision was made. What an auditor, funder or regulator will ask What source documents did the agent use for this item? Which version of the grant rules and which cost category definitions applied? Why was it classified this way? Who verified it, what did they see and when? Which model, prompt and configuration were in force? How many other items and projects were treated the same way? Has the record been altered since? Can you produce it for the full retention period? Why ordinary logs fail the funded organisation They rotate long before the retention period ends, which can be five years or more after final payment. They record outputs, not the sources, rules and versions behind them. They cannot list everything affected by one faulty rule. They do not show who reviewed what. They can be edited, and an auditor's first question about any record is whether it is original. They sit in vendor systems you may no longer have access to when the audit arrives. Step 1: map agent work to obligations Start with a register, not with technology. List every task an agent performs, and for each one record which obligation it touches. Agent task Obligation touched Evidence needed later Classify costs against grant categories Eligibility of costs, record keeping, audit Source docs, rule version, classification, reviewer Draft periodic technical or financial reports Reporting accuracy Inputs, draft, edits, approver Answer citizen or applicant questions Duty of care, transparency Question, sources used, answer, handoff Triage applications or benefits Fundamental rights, non-discrimination, explanation Inputs, criteria, outcome, human review Draft procurement documents Procurement rules Sources, changes, approver Handle incidents or alerts NIS2 reporting, security Timeline, actions, evidence For every row, name an owner. A task without an owner will not have evidence. Step 2: record decisions as linked chains tied to the funding context Each decision should be linked to the grant, work package or programme it affects, so that an audit by grant, by rule or by period is a query and not a project. python src = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="source_item", data={"grant": "HE-101012345", "wp": "WP3", "item_ref": "INV-77421", "doc_sha256": "", "period": "RP2"}) rule = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rules_applied", data={"grant_rules": "HE-MGA v1.2 Art 6", "national_rules": "UNI-POLICY-2026-04", "category_table_v": "9", "prompt_v": "v18", "model": "provider-model-2026-03"}, parent_id=src.id) cls = await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="classification", data={"category": "direct_equipment_service", "eligible": True, "basis": ["service contract used only for project equipment"], "confidence": "medium"}, parent_id=rule.id) Store references and digests of documents, not full copies, and apply redaction before storage for personal data. Step 3: separate agent judgment from verified decisions Where money or rights depend on a decision, record the human step with what the person saw. python rev = await db.log(agent="research-accounts", event="human_review", data={"reviewer": "u-acct-12", "saw": ["invoice", "contract", "classification_basis"], "action": "confirmed", "sample_type": "risk_based"}, parent_id=cls.id) Do not log only that someone clicked approve. Log what they were shown, what they changed and why. An auditor will weigh a review more heavily when it shows engagement with evidence. Step 4: add rules outside the model for the costly mistakes Put deterministic checks around the decisions that matter most. Examples for a research office: a cost above a threshold needs human review, a cost type flagged as ineligible by the programme's rules cannot be marked eligible by the agent, and an item that matches a known risky pattern, such as shared equipment or overheads, must be flagged. python await db.log(agent="grants-cost-agent", event="rule_check", data={"rule": "shared_equipment_needs_review", "result": "flag", "blocking": True}, parent_id=cls.id) A flagged item is held for review. The audit record explains afterwards. The rule prevents. Step 5: use impact queries to answer extension of findings When an auditor, or your own review, finds a faulty rule, prompt version or classification pattern, you need to know every item that used it, across every grant. python affected = await db.impact(rule.id) Use it before the funder asks. List the items, correct or document each, and approach the funder with a complete picture. Voluntarily scoping and correcting a problem is a stronger position than having it extended to you. Step 6: align retention with the funding clock Set retention from the longest obligation that applies, not from your IT default. Funding. At least the period in the grant agreement, such as five years after final payment for larger Horizon Europe grants, and longer if an audit is open or national rules require. Legal hold. When an audit, investigation or dispute starts, suspend deletion for the relevant records. Data protection. Keep personal data only as long as needed, and decide in advance how erasure requests interact with an integrity-protected record. ZizkaDB supports redaction before storage and forget with tombstones, and your data protection officer should approve the approach. Exportability. Export and archive before systems are retired, and test that archives can be re-imported and verified. python export = await db.export_events(agent="grants-cost-agent", since="2026-01-01", until="2026-06-30") Step 7: make the record tamper evident, with custody you can defend Every event in ZizkaDB carries a SHA-256 checksum chained to the previous one for that agent. Any edit, deletion or reordering breaks the chain. Verify on a schedule and store the chain head somewhere your own system administrators cannot edit, such as your records management system or your internal audit function. python check = await db.verify_chain(agent="grants-cost-agent") store check.head with internal audit, and log the verification date When an auditor asks whether the record is original, you can show a verification result and the independently held head. That proves the record has not changed since the head was stored. It does not prove the record was complete. Step 8: prepare for the incident clock If an agent is involved in a security or data incident, NIS2-type reporting starts at awareness: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report within one month. Prepare in advance. Make sure you can freeze and export the relevant chain, list every action the agent took in the window, scope affected records through the impact query, and show who did what during the response. Our incident response how-to covers the 72 hour runbook in more detail. Step 9: give auditors a clean, safe way in Create an audit access procedure before you need it. Use read-only, expiring keys scoped to the grant, period or decision set requested. Provide a standard export with the chain verification result. Keep a log of who accessed what. Run a dry audit once a year with someone outside the team. python await db.log(agent="audit-desk", event="auditor_access_granted", data={"auditor_org": "funder-audit-unit", "scope": "grant HE-101012345", "expires": "2026-12-31", "approved_by": "u-compliance-3"}) Step 10: choose infrastructure that fits public-sector constraints Publicly funded bodies often face procurement rules, data residency expectations, sovereignty concerns and vendor exit requirements. Design for them. Self host inside your own environment or an EU-based environment you control, so the evidence stays in your custody. Avoid lock-in. Choose tools that are open source, so your team and your auditors can inspect the code, and that are model, LLM and cloud agnostic, so you can change providers without losing history. Keep it small. A single container on Postgres is easier to secure, accredit and operate than a sprawling platform. Plan exit. Test exporting and re-importing your records. ZizkaDB's core is AGPL-3.0, runs self hosted in a single Docker container, and can be placed inside the environment you choose. Whether it meets your security and procurement requirements is for your own teams to decide. Business objectives and how to measure them Objective Measure Protect funding from recovery Share of audited items with a complete evidence chain; ineligible cost found per audit Cut audit preparation time Hours to answer an auditor request, before and after Contain a finding early Time from discovering a faulty rule to listing all affected items Support AI governance duties Share of agent decisions with a full record; FRIA evidence ready Strengthen future bids and procurement positions Evidence packs provided to funders and partners on request Reduce reputational risk Citizen complaints resolved with a verifiable account An illustrative exposure example This is invented, to show the logic. A university manages 40 EU and national grants worth 20 million euros over the reporting period. If a systematic classification weakness caused 2 percent of the claimed costs to be later found ineligible, the exposure would be 400,000 euros, before the cost of the audit itself and the staff time to rebuild evidence. Even a modest reduction in that risk, or in the time to scope it, can justify the effort of recording decisions properly. Use your own figures. Common mistakes Treating AI as an IT matter. The obligations belong to finance, research administration, legal and service owners, not only to the technology team. Keeping logs for 30 days and grants for 5 years. The shortest retention in the chain sets your real position. Letting an agent decide eligibility alone. Put rules and human review around money and rights. Recording output only. An auditor needs sources, rules and versions. Forgetting the review step. Show what the reviewer saw. One copy, one custodian. Store the chain head elsewhere. Assuming the vendor holds the evidence. If the contract ends, so can your access. Ignoring erasure. Decide the approach before the first request. A 30 day plan Days 1 to 5: build the obligation register. List agent tasks, the obligation each touches, the retention period that applies and an owner. Days 6 to 10: choose one high-value workflow, such as cost classification, and define its event model with research administration, legal and your data protection officer. Days 11 to 15: instrument the workflow with source, rules, classification and review events, and add the blocking rules for the highest risk items. Days 16 to 20: set retention and legal hold, test export and re-import, and verify the hash chain with the head held by internal audit. Days 21 to 25: run an impact query on a seeded faulty rule and measure how fast you can list affected items across grants. Days 26 to 30: run a mock audit with someone outside the team using the eight questions above. Record the gaps, assign owners and agree the next workflow. Where ZizkaDB fits, and its limits ZizkaDB is an open source causal audit database for AI agents. It records each decision as a linked event, answers why() for any outcome, lists everything downstream of a faulty input through the impact route, supports replay and drift baselines, and shows whether stored history has been altered through a SHA-256 hash chain. It is model, LLM and cloud agnostic, and it runs self hosted in a single Docker container, with a managed Cloud edition at db.zizka.ai for multi-agent setups. It does not decide whether a cost is eligible, assess fundamental rights impacts, report incidents or make a body compliant with any rule. It records what your system captures, so the rules and reviews you add are what prevent errors. The open source edition records one agent per install, so fleets and agent to agent flows use the Cloud edition or separate instances. Take advice from your legal, audit and data protection teams on retention, erasure and what the funder requires. If you rely on public money and use AI agents, choose one funded workflow this week and trace one claimed cost from the source document to the final report. If you can do it in minutes and show the record is original, you are ready for the audit. If you cannot, you have found the gap before the auditor did. title: Test swap: help my Android merge-idle game through Google Play closed testing (I test back)
summary: I'm a solo dev taking Moonbun Orbs through Google Play's closed testing (12 testers for 14 days). How to join (Android phone + Gmail) Join the Google Group with the same Gmail your Play Store uses: https://groups.google.com/g/moonbun-orbs-testers Open https://play.google.com/apps/testing/com.moonbunstudio.orbmerge , tap Become a tester , then install from Google Play. title: I almost gave up on local llms on low end hardware until I made these changes to my setup
summary: Squeezing Every Drop of Speed Out of a Laptop CPU: Recompiling ik_llama.cpp for Gemma 4 E2B + MTP + Pi After my previous findings, I almost called it quits on running models locally on my hardware: an AMD Ryzen 5 5625U with 16 GB dual-channel 3200 MHz RAM , locked to "Cool" mode with max processor state capped at 99% (~10–12W power limit, no turbo spikes). Before giving up, I looked into ternary models. I tried running Ternary Bonsai 2 9B , and it gave me similar performance to my Qwen 3.5 4B & 2B setup—around 6–10 tokens/sec (specifically ~6 tok/s on Bonsai). Token generation was still pretty slow. It wasn't horrible, but it wasn't great either. Then I saw a YouTube video about Gentoo Linux —the distro where you compile almost all software directly on your own hardware for a small performance boost. It reminded me of Formula 1: in F1, even shaving a few hundredths of a second off a lap time can be the difference between winning and losing. So I decided to recompile the inference engine myself. I ended up recompiling ikawrakow/ik_llama.cpp specifically for my Zen 3 CPU ( -O3 -march=znver3 -mtune=znver3 ) because it supports -rtr (run-time repacking) . In simple terms, -rtr reorganizes the model's weights in RAM into a neat 8-row interleaved layout tailored for Zen 3's AVX2 vector instructions, so the CPU can read and multiply weights much faster instead of unpacking them awkwardly on the fly. Choosing the Right Model & Tuning Threads After consulting with Gemini Hydrogen , I decided to go with Gemma 4 E2B (essentially ~4.6B total parameters / ~2.3B active compute). For my 16 GB dual-channel RAM setup, this hits the sweet spot for speed and accuracy. Even though its standalone coding isn't quite as strong as Qwen 3.5 4B with thinking on, it works great for my workflow because I use Hydrogen in Antigravity as the cloud orchestrator and run Gemma 4 locally with thinking turned off . The performance genuinely surprised me—I did not expect it to run this well on a 10–12W laptop cap. Because of the Cool-mode power limit, I ran llama-bench ( -ngl 0 -rtr 1 --no-mmap -fa 1 -p 512 -n 128 ) across 3, 4, 5, and 6 threads to find the sweet spot: Threads Prompt Processing ( pp512 ) Token Generation ( tg128 ) -t 3 111.69 tok/s 9.07 tok/s -t 4 142.74 tok/s 9.00 tok/s -t 5 166.83 tok/s 7.84 tok/s -t 6 143.93 tok/s 6.70 tok/s Using all 6 threads starved per-core clocks under the 10–12W cap and dropped generation to 6.70 tok/s . Splitting it to -t 4 for generation and -tb 5 for prompt processing gave me the best of both worlds. I'm sure if I switched to Performance or Balanced mode at 100% power it would get an even bigger boost, but I don't want to melt my laptop. Initially, I ran google_gemma-4-E2B-it-IQ4_NL.gguf ( 3.14 GiB , from bartowski ) because it uses slightly less RAM with similar accuracy, paired with the mtp-gemma-4-E2B-it-Q8_0.gguf ( ~95 MiB ) MTP speculative drafter. Even though the drafter cancelled out the small RAM savings, it was still much lighter than running a bigger model with MTP—and it hit 17.31 tok/s with a 94.1% draft acceptance rate (16/17 accepted) on a smoke test. Switching to the Uncensored Model Around a day later, I saw a video by Kai on YouTube about uncensored models and decided it made more sense to run the uncensored variant. I switched to: Main Model: gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-heretic.i1-Q4_0.gguf ( 3.12 GiB , from mradermacher , skipping mmproj to save RAM) MTP Drafter: gemma-4-E2B-it-assistant-Q8_0.gguf ( 94.81 MiB , from cafkafk ) The performance is fantastic: MTP Draft Acceptance Rate: 80.77% (21 accepted / 26 generated on JSON test) Token Generation: 13.04 – 15.39 tok/s (300 tokens of Python code in ~23s) Prompt Processing: 112.70 – 172.69 tok/s Memory Footprint: ~3.77 GB total ( 3181.5 MiB model + q8_0 KV cache at 16K context) + ~371 MB for the drafter, with all 271 main tensors and 23 drafter tensors repacked via -rtr . Launch Profiles & Offline Pi Harness I set up two .bat launchers—one with thinking turned off for when Hydrogen is orchestrating, and another with thinking turned on for standalone debugging: Shared Engine & Low-RAM Flags: - m "E:\models\gemma-4-E2B-it-qat-q4_0-unquantized-heretic.i1-Q4_0.gguf" ^ - md "E:\models\gemma-4-E2B-it-assistant-Q8_0.gguf" ^ -- spec - type mtp : n_max = 2 , p_min = 0.0 ^ - rtr -- no - mmap - ngl 0 - t 4 - tb 5 - c 16384 - np 1 ^ - ctk q8_0 - ctv q8_0 - fa on - b 512 - ub 256 -- jinja -- host 127.0 . 0.1 -- port 8080 (Using -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 halves KV cache memory, -np 1 keeps context to a single slot so RAM stays low, and --spec-type mtp:n_max=2,p_min=0.0 caps draft guesses at 2 so the CPU doesn't waste cycles verifying rejected tokens.) Thinking OFF ( start-gemma4-uncensored.bat — Fast Coding / Cloud-Orchestrated): --reasoning off --temp 0.4 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --repeat-penalty 1.1 Thinking ON ( start-gemma4-uncensored-thinking.bat — Complex Debugging): --reasoning on --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --repeat-penalty 1.0 I also set up Pi ( @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent ) with itayinbarr/little-coder (for just-in-time tool injection and small-model guardrails), the Pi Code GUI extension in VS Code, and a custom Pi extension that sandboxes file and bash tools strictly to my E:\ flash drive—so I still have a capable local coding assistant even when I'm offline or don't have access to cloud models. Looking forward to seeing what this uncensored local setup can help me build and create. Repo with all launch scripts & Pi configs: https://github.com/MVYNE06/gemma4-zen3-local-stack

title: Why CSS 1in = 96px Is Not 1 Physical Inch (Building a True 1:1 Screen Ruler in React)
summary: If you have ever tried setting width: 1in; or width: 10cm; in CSS and held a physical ruler up to your monitor, you probably noticed something frustrating: it is almost never 1 physical inch. On a 27-inch 4K monitor, a 13-inch MacBook Air, and a 6.7-inch Android phone, 1in in CSS can be off by 15% to 45% . Here is why browsers cannot reliably report physical millimeters out of the box, and how we built a true 1:1 actual-size online ruler and ring sizer in React using ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 credit-card PPI calibration . Why 1in , 1cm , and window.devicePixelRatio Cannot Give True Physical Size According to the W3C CSS Values and Units specification, 1in is locked to exactly 96 CSS pixels ( 1cm = 37.795px , 1mm = 3.7795px ). Wait - what about window.devicePixelRatio ? devicePixelRatio only tells you how many hardware pixels map to 1 CSS pixel (for example, 2 on Retina displays or 2.75 on high-DPI phones). It still does not tell JavaScript the physical diagonal size of the monitor or phone glass in inches! Browsers deliberately omit raw physical display dimensions (EDID data) to reduce browser fingerprinting . As a result: Display CSS 1in Real Physical Size of 96 CSS px Error Standard 24" 1080p Monitor 96px ~1.04 in +4% 13.3" MacBook Retina ( 2x ) 96px ~0.84 in -16% 6.5" Smartphone ( 3x ) 96px ~0.66 in -34% So if you build a browser ruler using static CSS cm or in units, it will be visibly wrong on almost every laptop and smartphone. The Reliable Fix: ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 Credit-Card Calibration Almost every person on Earth has a globally standardized physical reference object in their wallet: a standard bank card, debit card, or ID card . Under the ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1 international standard, every standard payment card has the exact same physical width: Width: 85.60 mm ( 8.56 cm / 3.370 inches ) Height: 53.98 mm ( 5.398 cm / 2.125 inches ) Instead of guessing the user's screen PPI, let the user hold a bank card flat against the screen and drag a slider until an on-screen card box matches the physical card edge-to-edge. Once cardWidthPx matches 3.37 physical inches, calculating the exact effective CSS Pixels Per Inch (PPI) takes one line of math: const STANDARD_CARD_INCHES = 3.37 ; // 85.60 mm (ISO/IEC 7810 ID-1) export function calculateEffectivePpi ( cardWidthPx : number ) : number { return cardWidthPx / STANDARD_CARD_INCHES ; } From that single calibrated ppi number, every physical unit becomes exact on that display: export function pxToPhysical ( px : number , ppi : number ) { const inches = px / ppi ; return { inches : Number ( inches . toFixed ( 2 ) ) , cm : Number ( ( inches * 2.54 ) . toFixed ( 2 ) ) , mm : Number ( ( inches * 25.4 ) . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , } ; } Persist that calibrated ppi in localStorage , and the user only ever has to calibrate once per device: const STORAGE_KEY = "omnitools_ruler_ppi" ; export function loadSavedPpi ( ) : number { try { const saved = localStorage . getItem ( STORAGE_KEY ) ; const parsed = saved ? parseFloat ( saved ) : NaN ; return Number . isFinite ( parsed ) && parsed >= 40 && parsed <= 300 ? parsed : 96 ; } catch { return 96 ; } } (Clamping between 40 and 300 prevents corrupted storage values from breaking the UI.) Bonus Use Case: An On-Screen Ring Size Finder (US, UK, and India Sizes) Once you know the true ppi of a screen, you can measure more than straight lines. You can render a calibrated circle where the user places an existing ring directly onto their phone or laptop glass and adjusts the circle diameter until it aligns with the inside edge of the ring: interface RingSizeEntry { mm : number ; us : string ; uk : string ; india : string ; } const RING_SIZES : RingSizeEntry [ ] = [ { mm : 14.9 , us : "4" , uk : "H" , india : "8" } , { mm : 15.7 , us : "5" , uk : "J 1/2" , india : "10" } , { mm : 16.5 , us : "6" , uk : "M" , india : "12" } , { mm : 17.3 , us : "7" , uk : "O" , india : "14" } , { mm : 18.2 , us : "8" , uk : "Q" , india : "17" } , { mm : 19.0 , us : "9" , uk : "S" , india : "19" } , { mm : 19.8 , us : "10" , uk : "T 1/2" , india : "22" } , { mm : 20.6 , us : "11" , uk : "V 1/2" , india : "25" } , ] ; export function matchRingSize ( diameterPx : number , ppi : number ) { const diameterMm = ( diameterPx / ppi ) * 25.4 ; const closest = RING_SIZES . reduce ( ( prev , curr ) => Math . abs ( curr . mm - diameterMm ) < Math . abs ( prev . mm - diameterMm ) ? curr : prev ) ; return { diameterMm : Number ( diameterMm . toFixed ( 1 ) ) , closest } ; } 3 Frontend Edge Cases to Watch Out For Browser Zoom ( Ctrl + / Ctrl - ): Remind users to keep browser zoom at 100% during calibration and measurement, because zooming scales CSS pixels without changing localStorage . Prevent Accidental Text Selection While Dragging Markers: Add select-none ( user-select: none ) and touch-action: none on draggable measurement handles so mobile Safari/Chrome does not scroll the viewport while dragging a marker. Sub-Pixel Rendering for 1mm Ticks: On standard displays, 1mm is roughly 3.78px . Always compute tick positions from mm * (ppi / 25.4) instead of rounding each step cumulatively, otherwise rounding drift compounds to 2-3mm across a 15cm ruler! Try the Live Browser Implementation We built this full calibrated ruler, dual red/blue measurement markers (horizontal and vertical), and US/UK/India ring sizer completely client-side with zero tracking or app downloads: Online Ruler (Actual Size 1:1 + Ring Size Finder): https://omnitools.net/tools/online-ruler Unit Converter (Length, Weight, Temp & Storage): https://omnitools.net/tools/unit-converter Have you ever run into CSS physical-unit bugs on HiDPI screens or print stylesheets? Drop your experience in the comments!

title: Building a Pure-TypeScript 13x13 Crossword CSP Solver and 100-Page Vector PDF Engine on Cloudflare Workers
summary: Turning a group of friends' inside jokes into a real, print-ready crossword keepsake book sounds simple until you try to run both puzzle generation and 100-page book typesetting inside a single edge Worker. When we built ClueBook and its interactive puzzle & sample PDF preview , our main constraint was keeping the entire pipeline—13x13 crossword solving, vector PDF interior layout, and computed-spine cover generation—in pure TypeScript on OpenNext Cloudflare Workers with zero Python runtimes or headless browsers. 1. Deterministic 13x13 Bitmask CSP Solver Contributor clues are short, irregular, and unpredictable. A naive backtracking solver easily stalls or blows past Worker CPU budgets on dense intersections. We split grid construction into two bounded stages: Skeleton placement : Personal answers are placed first with a strict cap of 3,500 skeleton steps to maximize crossings between contributor entries. Bitmask CSP fill : Remaining open slots are filled against an open-licensed SCOWL wordlist using bitmask domain filtering, capped at 8,000 CSP nodes per grid with a deterministic fallback so every generation completes predictably. Because the solver is deterministic for a given approved clue set, regenerating a book after moderation or order fulfillment always yields the exact same puzzles and answer keys. 2. 100-Page 6x9 Vector PDF in Under 200ms Instead of rendering HTML through Chromium (which adds cold starts and memory spikes), we build the entire 100-page 6x9 ( 450 x 666 pt with print bleed) interior and dynamic-spine cover wrap directly with pdf-lib : Vector grid lines, crisp clue numbering, dedication pages, and answer keys stream out without rasterization bloat. The 100-page interior renders in under 200ms and the cover wrap in under 30ms , avoiding long-term blob storage of customer content. 3. Idempotent Fulfillment on D1 Paid print orders move through an atomic compare-and-swap state transition in Cloudflare D1 ( paid -> submitting_to_lulu -> submitted_to_lulu ) backed by an idempotent Stripe webhook log, ensuring retried webhooks never create duplicate print jobs. You can test the live 13x13 solver and 3-page sample PDF layout directly in the ClueBook Preview or create a group puzzle at getcluebook.com .

title: AI Isn't Transforming Work, Because the System Hasn't Changed
summary: The speed is real. The change is not. A draft that took an hour now takes ten minutes. A summary arrives in seconds. A first version of anything is one prompt away. And yet the week feels the same. The same meetings. The same rework. That gap is the subject of this piece. AI is doing real work at the level of the single task. It is not, on its own, changing how work moves through a team. Those are two different things, and most teams have only touched the first one. A New Shape for Work opens with a plain diagnosis. AI is helpful, but it has not transformed the way most teams operate. The difference feels marginal. The reason, the guidebook says, is leverage. Used without a clear strategy, AI gives surprisingly little of it. The image the guidebook uses is a bicycle with one gear. "It's like adding a power boost to a bicycle with only one gear," the Introduction says, "the pedals move frenetically, but nothing has fundamentally changed." The pedals spin faster. The bike goes no faster. The rider works harder and arrives at the same place. Leverage is what lets you move up a level. The guidebook puts it this way: "Increased leverage allows you to move up to a higher level, and work on the system rather than in the system." That sentence is the whole argument in one line. Working in the system means doing the tasks faster. Working on the system means changing how the tasks flow and what survives them. Before and after The guidebook draws the contrast as a before and after list. Before: information scattered everywhere; everyone reinventing their own wheel; agents confused by outdated docs; one-off chats; isolated achievements. After: everything automatically organized; rationalized, shared systems; clean context for agents; automated processes; compounding flywheel. Read that list slowly. Nothing on the before side is a complaint about AI being weak. The AI works. The system around it does not. Outdated docs confuse agents. Scattered information means every task starts from zero. One-off chats mean nothing learned on Monday helps on Tuesday. Isolated achievements mean one person's win stays one person's win. The after side is not about a smarter model. It is about a shared system that holds what the team knows, so the model has something solid to work with. Organization comes first, automation second. That order matters. Automating a mess gives you a faster mess. Think about your own week. How much of it goes to finding things, re-explaining things, and redoing things? That is the tax of a system that has not changed. AI can cut the time each task takes, but it cannot cut the tax. Only a change to the system can do that. A faster draft does not fix a slow approval. A faster summary does not fix a meeting that should not exist. This is why the guidebook refuses to sell AI as a tool upgrade. A tool upgrade makes the same work faster. A system change makes different work possible. The first feels like progress for a month and then stalls. The second is slower to start and keeps paying. The core philosophy The guidebook states its core philosophy in plain terms: "Humans thrive when we do the creative work that we love, and that only we can do. Everything else can, should, and eventually will be automated." The question is how. The path has two parts. First, create a shared context system that your whole team and their agents can work in together. Second, create shared AI systems, sometimes called factories, that a handful of people can be responsible for, and that everyone else can benefit from. That sounds large. The guidebook insists it is not. The simplest version, it says, is nothing more than a shared to-do list with an agent and your team. That takes a few minutes to set up, and it can grow to handle tasks of near-infinite complexity. You do not need to change everything overnight. Start with one workflow, or one team. See if it works. Then go from there. That is the practical test hidden inside the philosophy. If the only place AI touches your work is inside private chats, the system has not changed. If one shared list exists, and an agent works from it, and the whole team can see the result, the system has started to change. When one part of a team adopts this way of working, the guidebook says, the rest quickly follow, without need for persuasion or change management. That claim is easy to test. It either happens or it does not. But it points to the real measure of success: not whether individuals use AI, but whether the team works differently because of it. What to do with this Pick one repeated piece of work. A weekly update. A status report. A triage step that happens every day. Give it a shared home instead of a private chat. Put the instructions and the expected output in one place the team can see. Let an agent run it from there. Watch what breaks, fix that one thing, and run it again. Do that, and you will learn more about your system in a week than a year of faster drafts will teach you. The drafts were never the problem. The system was. AI is not failing at work. It is waiting for the system to change. The bicycle needs another gear. The Matrix framed the same choice years ago. The blue pill is the faster draft in the same system. The red pill is changing the system itself. Transformation is a choice, not a tool swap.

title: Which LXD Deployments Actually Expose CVE-2026-135384?
summary: Which LXD Deployments Actually Expose CVE-2026-135384? An LXD version string is the beginning of a vulnerability assessment, not the end. CVE-2026-135384 only matters through the OIDC authentication path described by Canonical, and several deployment choices determine whether an affected release is reachable by a remote token. Canonical marks LXD releases before 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2 as affected. The vulnerability is CWE-287 improper authentication. The CNA assigned CVSS 4.0 score 9.2 Critical, while the GitHub advisory page shows a CVSS 3.1 score of 8.1 High. Both scores describe the same OIDC token boundary, but the practical question is whether a particular server uses that boundary. Start with the authentication mode LXD supports OIDC for web UI and CLI access. The documentation separately describes local Unix socket access and remote API authentication. A server that does not use OIDC is outside this CVE's described verification path, even if its LXD version falls within the affected range. Administrators should determine whether oidc.issuer , oidc.client.id , and related OIDC settings are present. The presence of an SSO button or a browser login page is useful evidence, but configuration records and the server version provide a more reliable inventory. Separate reachability from configuration Remote HTTPS exposure can make the API reachable, but it does not prove that OIDC is enabled. A server can expose the API with certificate authentication, restrict management to a trusted network, or accept only local administrative connections. Each of those deployments needs the version assessment, but the CVE's token-validation path requires the OIDC condition described by the advisory. The reverse is also important. A server may use OIDC and have an affected version but not be reachable by the attacker who holds a signed token. Network controls, management-interface restrictions, and provider trust boundaries affect exposure. They do not remove the need to patch, because an effective token presented to an internal endpoint still crosses the authentication boundary. The configuration conditions in the advisory The advisory says LXD checked issuer, signature, and expiry but, unless oidc.audience was set, did not bind a token to the LXD server. It also describes acceptance of a token without a named user, acceptance of an ID token in place of an access token, and use of unverified email claims. These details turn the audit into a review of identity-provider and LXD settings. An administrator should know whether the provider emits a distinct audience for LXD, whether the server requires it, which token type reaches the API, and how user names and groups are mapped. The advisory recommends setting oidc.audience to an LXD-only value. It recommends using a non-user-editable oidc.claim , such as sub , or configuring the provider to release only verified email addresses. These controls matter even while a fixed release is waiting to be deployed. Scope by release line The fixed versions are 5.0.12, 5.21.10, and 6.10.2. A deployment on an unsupported or custom build cannot rely on those boundaries without vendor confirmation. A deployment that has been patched should also confirm that the running binary, snap, or package is the fixed one and not an older artifact left in the active boot path. The CVE record lists affected ranges beginning at 5.0. Older LXD releases should not be assumed unaffected merely because they are outside the stated range. The authoritative record and vendor support status are the appropriate basis for a decision. Impact if the deployment matches The official advisory says any caller with a signed token from the configured issuer could authenticate, including a token that was issued to another application. In the default configuration without OpenFGA or a scriptlet, an authenticated OIDC client has full control of the server. With delegated authorization, the impact depends on the mapped permissions. Unauthorized access to LXD is operationally significant because the API manages containers, virtual machines, storage, and network configuration. A server administrator should treat the CVE as a control-plane authentication issue rather than a narrow login-page bug. Using ZoomEye without overstating it The frozen ZoomEye query for this topic returned 12,271 matches for app="LXD" and zero for vul.cve="CVE-2026-135384" . The first number shows that LXD fingerprints are visible in the product search. It does not show vulnerable software, OIDC use, token configuration, or host control. The zero CVE result is also not proof that no vulnerable systems exist. It means the selected CVE field did not produce a match in that query at that time. The article should use these observations to support inventory questions, not to claim a count of vulnerable or compromised deployments. A practical assessment sequence Begin with an asset inventory that records LXD version, deployment packaging, management address, and authentication mode. Mark affected versions for upgrade. For OIDC servers, capture issuer, audience, claim, group mapping, and authorization mechanism. Next, validate that external management access is intentional and restricted. Confirm the server does not accept tokens from unrelated clients, that ID tokens are rejected as access credentials, and that user claims resolve to the intended identities. These checks should be done with test accounts and recorded against the server build. Finally, monitor authentication changes after remediation. A successful patch addresses the code path, but the provider and server configuration still need to agree on audience, token type, and identity mapping. Remediation does not end with the version number Upgrade to 5.0.12, 5.21.10, or 6.10.2 according to the support line. Restart the service as required and verify the running version. Then re-run the configuration checks, because a fixed binary with an overly broad identity mapping can still create a security problem. The advisory's workarounds are useful for staged upgrades but are not permanent relief from the patched release. Treat them as documented compensating controls and validate them in the same identity-provider path used by production users.
