title: Stop Building “Remote Controls.” Build an Automation Engine
summary: Most smart home projects stall at the same point. You buy a smart plug. You open the app. You tap a button. The lamp turns on. It feels like progress — until you realize you have built a very expensive remote control. The STONE article on smart home automation draws a distinction that every developer should internalize before writing a single line of integration code: a smart device responds to a command; an automated home evaluates a condition and acts without anyone asking. The gap between those two things is not hardware. It is architecture. The Loop You Are Actually Building A functioning automation system is a closed loop. Sensors produce state. A logic layer evaluates that state against rules. Actuators receive commands. The loop runs continuously, mostly without human input. In a developer-friendly stack, that loop maps cleanly onto three concerns: Ingestion: devices publish state to a message bus. Evaluation: a rule engine subscribes to that bus and decides what should happen. Dispatch: commands go back out to the devices that can change the physical world. The mistake is collapsing these into a single process. When your sensor firmware directly calls your light’s HTTP endpoint, you have created a point-to-point dependency that breaks the moment either device changes, goes offline, or gets replaced. The MQTT pub/sub model exists precisely to decouple these concerns: devices publish to a broker; the logic layer subscribes; neither side needs to know the other’s address. Home Assistant as the Evaluation Layer, Not the Whole System Home Assistant is often described as a “hub,” which undersells what it actually is. Architecturally, it is a local-first event loop that integrates thousands of device protocols — Matter, Zigbee, Z-Wave, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth — and exposes them as entities that automations can reason about. It is the evaluation layer. It is not the message bus, and it is not the device. The cleaner design separates them. Run an MQTT broker (Mosquitto is the obvious starting point) as the message backbone. Let devices — ESP32 sensors, Tasmota-flashed plugs, Zigbee bridges — publish state to that broker. Let Home Assistant subscribe, evaluate, and publish commands back. The result is a system where you can swap a Zigbee temperature sensor for a Wi-Fi one without rewriting the automation that depends on it, because the automation is subscribed to a topic, not to a device. MQTT Discovery Is the Glue Worth Learning The single highest-leverage implementation detail in this stack is MQTT Discovery. Instead of manually defining every sensor in configuration files, a device publishes a retained JSON payload to a discovery topic. Home Assistant picks it up and creates the entity automatically. A minimal discovery payload for a temperature sensor looks like this: Published to homeassistant/sensor/livingroom_temp/config, this payload registers the entity, binds it to a physical device, and makes it available to automations without any manual YAML. The device becomes self-describing. That property matters more than it first appears: it means the automation layer does not need to be redeployed when hardware changes. The Automation Itself Should Be Boring Once the plumbing is in place, automations should read like state machines, not scripts. A trigger fires on a state transition. Conditions constrain the context. Actions dispatch commands. This is deliberately unglamorous. It is also deterministic, idempotent, and debuggable. When it fails — and it will — you can inspect three separate concerns: did the sensor publish? did the condition evaluate correctly? did the action reach the actuator? The Real Lesson Smart home automation is not a hardware problem. The devices are cheap and increasingly interoperable. The hard part is resisting the urge to build point-to-point remote controls and instead investing in a decoupled loop where state flows into a bus, logic evaluates it, and commands flow back out. Build that loop once, and every device you add afterward becomes a new input or output — not a new integration project.

title: The Swap Is the Easy Part: What Really Happens Between Clicking Exchange and Receiving Your Tokens?
summary: TronSeven — Non-Custodial Token Swaps on TRON Network Swap TRC-20 tokens on TRON with self-custody and open-source smart contracts. Low fees, verifiable on TRONSCAN. tronseven.com Most crypto users have experienced the same moment. You select two tokens, enter an amount, check the estimated output, connect your wallet, and click Swap. A few seconds later, the transaction appears in your wallet history. Simple, right? But between that button click and the arrival of your tokens, several important things happen. Your wallet communicates with the blockchain, a smart contract executes instructions, network resources are consumed, and the resulting transaction becomes part of a public ledger. Understanding this process changes how you evaluate crypto swap platforms. Instead of asking only, "How quickly can I exchange these tokens?", a better question is: Can I understand and verify what happens to my assets during the exchange? Let's explore that question from a practical TRON ecosystem perspective. A Token Swap Is More Than a Price Conversion Traditional currency conversion is relatively easy to understand. You exchange one currency for another using an agreed exchange rate. Blockchain swaps introduce additional layers. When exchanging TRC-20 tokens on TRON, the process generally involves: A wallet that authorizes the transaction. Token contracts representing the assets. A smart contract responsible for executing the swap. Network resources required to process the transaction. Blockchain confirmation and transaction records. Each component has a different responsibility. The wallet authorizes actions. The smart contract executes predefined logic. The TRON network processes the transaction and records its result. This distinction matters because a user is not simply exchanging two numbers on a screen. They are authorizing an on-chain operation. What Happens After You Click Swap? Let's break the process into understandable stages. Stage One: Transaction preparation The interface collects the selected tokens, the amount, and the expected output. Depending on the protocol, it may also calculate a route, estimate price impact, and account for slippage. These values help the user understand the proposed transaction before signing. Stage Two: Wallet authorization The application requests permission from the connected wallet to submit the transaction. This is an important security checkpoint. A wallet signature should never be treated as a routine confirmation without understanding what is being authorized. Always review the transaction details and make sure the requested action matches your intention. Stage Three: Smart contract execution The transaction reaches the relevant smart contract. The contract processes the instructions according to its programmed logic. If the required conditions are satisfied, the exchange can execute. Otherwise, the transaction may fail. Stage Four: Blockchain confirmation The TRON network processes the transaction. Once confirmed, the resulting transaction can be inspected using a blockchain explorer such as TRONSCAN. This provides an independent way to examine what happened instead of relying exclusively on an application's interface. Why TRON Energy and Bandwidth Matter One interesting aspect of the TRON ecosystem is its resource model. TRON uses two important resources: Bandwidth Bandwidth is used to account for the size of transactions and the data they contain. Energy Energy is primarily required for executing smart contract operations. A token swap involving TRC-20 contracts can consume Energy, while the transaction itself also uses network resources. This is one reason why comparing swap services solely by their advertised exchange rates can be misleading. The real cost of an operation may involve several components: Network resource consumption. Liquidity-related costs. Price impact. Any applicable service fees. A transparent interface should help users understand the relevant costs before they authorize a transaction. Slippage: The Difference Between Expectation and Execution Imagine that you want to exchange 1,000 USDT for another token. The interface displays an estimated amount you should receive. However, blockchain transactions do not always execute at the exact price displayed when the transaction was prepared. Market conditions can change. Liquidity can shift. Other transactions can affect the execution price. This is where slippage becomes important. Slippage represents the difference between the expected execution price and the actual execution price. A user should understand the following concepts before confirming an exchange: Expected output: The estimated amount of tokens to receive. Minimum received: The minimum output accepted by the transaction, where applicable. Price impact: How the trade itself affects the available market price. Slippage tolerance: The permitted deviation from the expected execution conditions. Setting slippage too tightly can cause transactions to fail. Setting it too loosely can expose users to worse execution than anticipated. The goal is not to choose the largest tolerance. It is to understand the trade-off. Blockchain Transparency Is a Practical Security Tool One of the most valuable characteristics of public blockchains is that transactions can be independently inspected. For TRON users, TRONSCAN provides a way to investigate transaction records. Instead of trusting a notification saying that a swap was successful, users can examine the underlying transaction. Useful details include: Transaction status. Transaction hash. Contract interactions. Token transfers. Addresses involved. Block information. Resource consumption. This does not automatically prove that a protocol is safe. A successful transaction only confirms that the blockchain processed the operation. It does not establish that the smart contract has no vulnerabilities or that the service is trustworthy. That distinction is essential. Blockchain transparency is a verification tool, not a universal security guarantee. Five Questions to Ask Before Using Any Swap Platform Before connecting a wallet to a new exchange interface, consider these questions: Is the smart contract publicly identifiable? You should be able to locate the relevant contract address and inspect its on-chain activity. Can the contract source code be verified? Verified source code makes it easier for independent researchers to examine contract logic. Is there meaningful security documentation? Look for details about audits, their scope, the reviewed contract versions, and any disclosed limitations. An audit is useful evidence, but it is not a guarantee against future vulnerabilities. Are the transaction costs understandable? A clear interface should distinguish estimated output, network costs, price impact, and applicable fees. Do you retain control of your wallet? Understand whether a service is custodial or non-custodial, what permissions it requests, and what happens to your assets during execution. Never share your seed phrase or private keys with a swap service. The Future of Crypto Swaps Is About Better Decisions The next generation of crypto swap interfaces should not compete exclusively on speed. Speed matters, but it is only one part of the experience. Users also need: Clear transaction information. Understandable fee structures. Verifiable smart contracts. Better wallet interaction. Meaningful security documentation. Transparent execution details. The best swap experience is one where users understand what they are authorizing rather than blindly trusting a confirmation button. This is particularly important as the TRON ecosystem continues to support a growing range of tokens, applications, and decentralized financial activities. Final Thoughts A crypto swap may look like a simple exchange, but it represents a coordinated interaction between wallets, smart contracts, network resources, and blockchain infrastructure. Understanding these layers is one of the most useful skills a crypto user can develop. The next time you exchange tokens, take a moment to look beyond the displayed rate. Check the transaction. Understand the permissions. Review the contract. Verify the result. Because in decentralized finance, the ability to verify what happened is just as important as the ability to make it happen.

title: How to send HubSpot deal stages to the Meta Conversions API
summary: Your campaign records leads. HubSpot records who qualified and who bought. Unless something connects the two, Meta never learns which leads turned into customers, and keeps optimizing for whoever fills in the form. Key points When a deal changes stage in HubSpot, send an event to the Meta Conversions API: Qualified , Disqualified and Purchase with the deal amount. The identifiers that let Meta match the event ( fbc , fbp , or the Lead Ads ID) must be stored when the lead is created . They can't be recovered later. In HubSpot, store them on the contact , then follow the deal's association to read them. Use action_source: system_generated , custom_data.event_source: "crm" and a stable event_id per deal and stage. Check HubSpot's native Meta events first. If they cover your case, you may not need any code. Step 1: store the identifier when the lead is born This is the step that can't be fixed later. For leads from your site, save the _fbc and _fbp cookies, plus email and phone, into contact properties at submission. For leads from Meta's instant forms, save the leadgen_id . Create contact properties with clear internal names, for example meta_fbc , meta_fbp and meta_lead_id . Your code always uses the internal name, never the label. Two details catch most people: _fbc only exists when the visitor arrived with an fbclid in the URL, and it only works within the same domain. Step 2: detect stage changes With a HubSpot Service Key (legacy private apps can no longer be created), there are no webhooks, so a small bot polls the deals search endpoint every few minutes for deals modified since the last run, filtered by your pipeline. For each deal that reached a tracked stage, it reads the deal's associated contact and takes the identifiers from there. Compare stages by their internal ID ( closedwon , or a numeric ID in custom pipelines), never by label. Step 3: build the Conversions API event The payload has four details that decide whether Meta uses it: action_source is system_generated ; custom_data carries lead_event_source (your CRM name) and event_source: "crm" ; user_data has lead_id for instant-form leads, or fbc and fbp in plain text plus email and phone hashed with SHA-256; event_id is stable per deal and stage, like <deal id>_won , so a reprocessed run doesn't count twice. For Purchase, add value and currency from the deal. HubSpot returns amount as a string and it may be empty when the stage moves before the rep fills it in, so wait a cycle instead of sending zero. Step 4: keep outbound out of the signal If the same pipeline gets paid leads and prospecting or referral deals, check for a paid-origin mark before sending anything. Otherwise every outbound sale becomes a Purchase credited to your campaigns. Where to start Start with Purchase: it's the only event with real value. Add Qualified next. If your funnel closes few deals a month, keep the campaign optimizing on a higher-volume event and use Purchase to judge quality. The 4-Layer Tracking Kit has this bot ready in Python, built for HubSpot's 2026-03 API, plus the three layers before it (browser, web GTM and server-side GTM with deduplication) and a 12-step validation ladder. FAQ Isn't HubSpot's native Meta integration enough? Sometimes. HubSpot can send ad conversion events to Meta based on lifecycle stage changes and HubSpot form submissions, on Marketing Hub Starter and above. It doesn't cover deal stages in any pipeline, forms outside HubSpot or a pixel that lives in GTM with server-side tracking. Don't run both for the same conversions, or Meta receives each one twice. What action_source should a CRM event use? system_generated. The event didn't happen in a browser. Also include custom_data.lead_event_source with your CRM name and custom_data.event_source set to crm, otherwise Meta may accept the event and not use it for lead optimization. Should fbc and fbp be hashed? No. Click and browser identifiers go in plain text. Only personal data like email and phone are hashed with SHA-256. title: Before the Transaction Happens: Why AML Screening Belongs Inside Crypto Infrastructure

Free tier included. amldark.com There is an interesting contradiction at the heart of cryptocurrency infrastructure. Blockchain networks are becoming faster, wallets are becoming easier to use, and payment systems are increasingly automated. A transfer that once required several manual steps can now be initiated through a simple API call. But there is one question that many systems still struggle to answer: Should this transaction be allowed to proceed in the first place? In many crypto workflows, risk checks happen after a deposit arrives, after funds enter a processing pipeline, or even after a suspicious transaction has already been completed. That approach creates an architectural problem. If compliance is treated as a separate administrative function rather than part of transaction processing, the system may discover important risks too late. Let's explore a different approach. The transaction lifecycle needs a security checkpoint Consider a relatively common scenario. A cryptocurrency payment platform accepts USDT deposits. Its infrastructure monitors incoming transfers, updates customer balances, and automatically processes withdrawals. Everything works as expected from a technical perspective. The transaction is valid. The address exists. The network confirms the transfer. The smart contract interaction succeeds. However, technical validity and financial risk are two different questions. A blockchain can confirm that a transaction happened. It cannot independently establish that every participant in the transaction chain represents an acceptable business risk. This is why transaction processing should include a separate risk-assessment stage. A simplified lifecycle could look like this: A customer initiates a deposit or withdrawal. The system identifies the blockchain network and relevant address. The compliance layer evaluates available risk indicators. The system assigns an appropriate processing status. A transaction proceeds, receives additional review, or is temporarily held according to the platform's policies. The important architectural change is the position of the compliance layer. Instead of being an emergency response mechanism, it becomes part of the normal transaction lifecycle. Why a wallet address is not enough One of the most common mistakes in blockchain risk assessment is treating an address as an isolated object. An address has a balance and a transaction history, but its wider context can be much more informative. For example, consider three hypothetical wallets: Wallet A receives funds from established exchange infrastructure. Wallet B regularly interacts with unidentified counterparties. Wallet C has indirect exposure to addresses associated with previously identified high-risk activity. All three wallets can technically receive and send USDT. Yet their risk profiles may be very different. This is where blockchain analytics becomes important. A more useful assessment considers several dimensions: Direct exposure: Is the address itself associated with a known sanctions designation, freeze record, or other relevant risk indicator? Indirect exposure: Are there connections to higher-risk addresses through previous transactions? Transaction behavior: Are there unusual patterns involving transfer frequency, amounts, or repeated movements between related addresses? Counterparty context: What information is available about the entities participating in the transaction? Data freshness: How recently were the relevant intelligence sources updated? No single indicator should automatically replace a complete investigation. A suspicious connection is a reason to understand the context, not necessarily proof of wrongdoing. The importance of network-specific intelligence Not all blockchain networks should be analyzed in exactly the same way. This becomes particularly relevant when working with stablecoins. USDT operates across multiple blockchain environments, including TRON, Ethereum, BNB Chain, Solana, and TON. Although the asset carries the same ticker, the underlying transaction infrastructure is different. TRC20 transfers, for example, operate within the TRON ecosystem and have their own network mechanics, address activity patterns, and transaction graph characteristics. An analytics system designed without considering these differences may overlook important details. A robust screening architecture should therefore account for: The actual network used for the transfer. Token-specific transaction activity. Relevant address relationships. Network-specific behavioral patterns. Cross-chain movements where reliable attribution is available. This is especially important for businesses processing substantial amounts of TRC20 USDT. A generic address lookup is not necessarily equivalent to a meaningful blockchain risk assessment. Build a risk decision, not just a risk score A numerical risk score is useful because it makes information easier to interpret. However, a number alone is not a compliance strategy. Imagine that an address receives a score of 42 out of 100. What should happen next? Should the transaction be rejected? Should it proceed? Does it require additional information? Without a defined decision process, the score provides limited operational value. A better approach is to establish three possible outcomes. Low risk — Standard processing No relevant high-risk indicators have been identified within the scope of the screening performed. The transaction can follow the platform's normal processing rules. Medium risk — Additional review Some indicators require clarification. The system can request enhanced due diligence, additional counterparty information, or manual compliance review. High risk — Escalation Significant risk indicators have been identified. The platform can temporarily hold the transaction, escalate the case, and follow its internal compliance procedures. The exact thresholds should be determined by the organization's risk model and applicable requirements. Most importantly, a score should never be presented as an absolute guarantee that funds are safe or unsafe. Good compliance architecture combines automated analysis with documented human decision-making. The API is where compliance becomes infrastructure For developers, one of the most interesting aspects of AML automation is integration. A standalone screening dashboard can be useful, but its operational value increases when risk assessment becomes accessible to the applications already processing transactions. For example, an exchange could integrate address screening into its deposit workflow. An OTC platform could evaluate a counterparty before accepting a transfer. A payment processor could introduce additional verification before releasing funds. A custody platform could periodically review addresses under its management. This creates an opportunity to make compliance more consistent across different parts of the infrastructure. However, API integration should be designed carefully. A production-ready workflow needs to consider: Authentication and access control. Request timeouts and retry policies. Rate limits. Monitoring and alerting. Error handling. Audit logs. Data retention. Manual escalation procedures. There is also an important distinction between a successful API response and a successful compliance decision. If a screening service becomes unavailable, the application should not automatically interpret that situation as a clean result. A system should have an explicitly defined fallback policy for unavailable screening data. Depending on the business model and risk appetite, this could mean temporarily holding a transaction or routing it for manual review. Failing safely is an important part of financial infrastructure. What does this look like in practice? This is where specialized blockchain screening platforms become relevant. One example is AMLdark, which focuses on cryptocurrency address risk assessment, particularly TRC20 USDT activity. Its platform describes screening against sanctions-related information, Tether freeze records, darknet datasets, and other risk intelligence sources. It also provides address-level risk information and supports API-based integration for businesses that want to incorporate screening into their existing workflows. Another interesting aspect is its focus on the TRON ecosystem rather than treating every blockchain as interchangeable. For developers and compliance teams working with substantial TRC20 USDT flows, network-specific screening can be an important consideration. More information about its functionality and available screening options can be found at: AMLdark — Cryptocurrency AML Screening As with any compliance product, businesses should independently evaluate data coverage, update frequency, integration requirements, and suitability for their particular regulatory environment. The bigger architectural lesson There is a broader lesson here that goes beyond AML software. Modern financial applications increasingly depend on automated decision-making. Payment authorization, fraud detection, identity verification, transaction monitoring, and compliance checks are becoming interconnected components of the same infrastructure. Treating them as completely separate processes creates unnecessary operational gaps. The next generation of crypto infrastructure should be designed around a simple principle: A transaction should not be considered fully processed simply because the blockchain accepted it. Technical confirmation and business acceptance are different stages. By placing risk assessment earlier in the transaction lifecycle, organizations can make more informed decisions, improve operational consistency, and create better records of how those decisions were reached. Blockchain technology makes value transfer programmable. It is time to make risk management an equally deliberate part of that architecture. Final thought If you are building an exchange, payment gateway, OTC platform, or another application that handles stablecoin transfers, consider where your AML screening actually happens. Is it part of the transaction workflow, or is it something your team only checks when a problem appears? That architectural decision may matter more than another optimization to your transaction-processing speed. What do you think: should AML screening be a mandatory pre-transaction component of modern crypto infrastructure, or should it remain a separate monitoring function? I'd be interested in hearing how other developers approach this problem.

title: Best robot dog for oil and gas site inspection: B2, X30, A2 or Spot
summary: Short answer: For oil and gas rounds outside classified hazardous zones, the Unitree B2 (40 kg rated payload) or DEEP Robotics X30 (20 kg, IP67 per its maker) is usually the practical choice for a full thermal, gas and acoustic payload; the Unitree A2 suits lighter payloads at lower cost, and Spot (14 kg) suits teams that value its software ecosystem. Do not assume any standard version is certified for explosive atmospheres. Start with the area classification, not the robot The first question on any oil and gas site is where the robot will walk. Tank farms, compressor stations, wellpads and process units are often split into classified zones (for example Zone 1 and Zone 2 under IECEx or ATEX). A robot that enters a classified zone needs an explosion-protection certificate for that zone, and so does every sensor on its back. Ask the robot maker for the certificate covering the exact model and zone; do not rely on an IP rating, which only covers dust and water. Many operators start with routes that stay in unclassified areas or are run under a work permit with gas monitoring, and use the robot for the repetitive parts: walking the same route every shift, logging gauge values, taking thermal images of pumps and motors and sniffing for leaks. That is the job the four robots below are compared for. The four robots side by side Robot Own weight Rated payload Built-in perception Maker's protection rating Best fit on an oil and gas site Unitree B2 60 kg 40 kg 3D LiDAR, front and rear depth cameras IP67 Heavy multi-sensor payloads, long outdoor routes DEEP Robotics X30 56 kg 20 kg Front and rear LiDAR, depth and wide-angle cameras IP67 Industrial routes in rain, dust and at night Unitree A2 37 kg 25 kg Front and rear LiDAR, HD camera Check with the maker Medium payloads where cost and handling weight matter Boston Dynamics Spot 32.7 kg 14 kg 5 stereo camera pairs Check with the maker Teams that value its existing software and integrations Weights and payloads are the manufacturers' published figures. The rated payload is an upper limit; real routes with stairs, grating and slopes go better well below it. Unitree B2 carrying a YUANZHI ROBOTICS sensor payload (3D render) What an oil and gas inspection payload actually weighs The robot choice usually follows from the payload. A typical oil and gas round combines four jobs: thermal checks on rotating equipment, gas detection, acoustic leak finding and reading analog gauges. Some real component figures: Dual-spectrum PTZ (Hikvision DS-2TD5566T-15/V2): about 4.5 kg and 18 W. Zoom for gauges and radiometric thermal for bearings and motors in one unit. Acoustic imager (CRYSOUND CRY8124): about 1.4 kg; the Fluke SV600 is lighter at about 0.85 kg. Acoustic imaging finds compressed-gas and steam leaks that a thermal camera cannot see. Multi-gas module (Winsen ZCE04B, four gases including CO and H2S): about 50 g and 0.5 W. Light and cheap, but it only measures the air that reaches it, so mounting position and airflow matter. Navigation LiDAR (Livox Mid-360): 265 g and 6.5 W, if the robot's own sensors are not enough for your mapping needs. Onboard compute (Jetson Orin NX 16GB class): budget up to around 40 W at peak for gauge-reading and detection models. Add brackets, an enclosure, cabling and a 5G or mesh radio, and a full thermal, acoustic, gas and PTZ payload can reach 8 to 10 kg. On a B2 that is a comfortable fraction of the rating. On an X30 or A2 it fits, but you trade some runtime. On Spot you are close to the limit and will usually swap the large PTZ for a lighter camera. Our weight and power budget guide shows how to add this up for your own list. Optical gas imaging view of a leak plume during a robot dog patrol (scene from the YUANZHI ROBOTICS product film) Gas detection: point sensors, acoustic or optical gas imaging Point gas sensors confirm a concentration where the robot is standing; they do not show where the leak is. Acoustic imagers locate pressurized leaks by sound, even in noisy plants, but say nothing about which gas it is. Optical gas imaging (OGI) cameras make hydrocarbon plumes visible and are the most direct way to find methane and VOC leaks, but cooled OGI cameras are heavy, power-hungry and expensive, which pushes you towards the B2. Many sites combine a point sensor for alarms with an acoustic imager for localisation. Our thermal vs optical gas imaging guide explains what each camera can and cannot detect. Terrain, weather and the route Grating and stairs: process units are full of open-mesh grating and steep steel stairs. All four robots can climb stairs, but check foot slip on wet grating during your trial and keep the payload's centre of mass low and central. Rain, dust and heat: the B2 and X30 carry IP67 ratings from their makers, but the payload enclosure, connectors and camera windows must be sealed to match. A rated robot with an unsealed payload is only as good as the payload. GNSS and localization: open sites suit RTK GNSS; dense pipe racks block satellites and need LiDAR localization. Most real routes need both. Night rounds: thermal works in the dark, but gauge reading needs light. Plan an illuminator and test reading accuracy at night, not just during the day. Robot dog gimbal reading analog pressure gauges at an inspection point How to choose Map the route and mark every classified zone. If the robot must enter Zone 1 or Zone 2, start by asking each maker which certified variant exists. List the payload you really need and total its weight and power before you pick the robot. If the total is above roughly 10 kg or includes a cooled OGI camera, shortlist the B2. Between about 5 and 10 kg, the X30 and A2 are both reasonable. Below that, Spot also works. Run a pilot on your worst stretch of route (wet grating, stairs, pipe racks) before committing to a fleet. Our pilot project guide covers what to measure.
